input.description: First-principles analysis of job relocation decision
input.prompt:
Help a user reason through a personal career/relocation decision from first principles. This is not a coding task — it's a life decision analysis. Decompose the problem into verified ground truths, surface and challenge the hidden assumptions, and reason upward to a recommendation (or a clear framework for deciding, if the inputs are too personal/unknown for a single answer).

Situation:
- User is a software engineer, 5 years at their current employer, based in Portland, OR, currently in a fully remote role.
- A large San Francisco tech company has offered them a new job: +$70K/year total comp (base + equity combined) over current compensation.
- The new job requires relocating to the SF Bay Area and working 3 days/week in-office (hybrid).
- User's partner has an established, Portland-based career with no remote option for that partner's work — meaning relocation would force the partner to either quit, find a new job in the Bay Area, or the couple would need to commute/live apart.
- No other details given (ages, kids, savings, visa status, housing situation, how replaceable the partner's job is, risk tolerance, how much the user likes their current job, career trajectory goals, etc.) — treat unknowns as unknowns rather than inventing specifics.

What to do:
1. Decompose into the real underlying decision variables (comp delta after cost-of-living adjustment, career/equity upside, relationship/partner career cost, quality-of-life/commute cost, reversibility of the decision, optionality value of staying vs. going).
2. Apply inversion, second-order thinking, and a pre-mortem: what would make this decision obviously wrong in 2 years? What's being assumed that shouldn't be (e.g., that $70K raw delta is the real economic delta once SF Bay Area cost of living, taxes, and commute time are netted out; that equity is worth face value; that remote-with-no-equity-upside is a stable baseline; that the partner's career is truly non-transferable; that 3 days/week in-office is the binding constraint rather than the relocation itself).
3. Estimate the real magnitude of the comp delta after Bay Area cost-of-living adjustment (rent/housing especially) — rough Fermi estimate is fine, cite it as an estimate.
4. Surface the asymmetry: this is a two-body/joint decision, not just a personal comp optimization — the partner's career cost is a real economic and relational cost even though it doesn't show up in the offer letter.
5. Give a trade-off framing (not a prescriptive "yes take it" or "no don't") — the goal is to equip the user with the structure to decide, since only they know their risk tolerance, relationship priorities, and how replaceable the partner's job is.

Output format: a tight, readable analysis (not a wall of headers) ending in a short, concrete recommendation of what questions the user and their partner should answer together before deciding, plus a one-line bottom-line steer if the first-principles math points clearly one direction. Keep it under ~500 words — this will be relayed directly to the user in a chat, not stored as a document.

Links: [{"title":"US Tax Tools","url":"https://ustax.tools/california-vs-oregon-taxes/"},{"title":"Moving from California to Oregon (2026) - cost & tax comparison","url":"https://globalcostdata.com/us/relocation/california-to-oregon/"},{"title":"article 11289 dr know","url":"https://www.wweek.com/portland/article-11289-dr-know.html"},{"title":"United States · 2025","url":"https://www.brackets.tax/united-states/compare/oregon-vs-california/2025"},{"title":"United States · 2025","url":"https://www.brackets.tax/united-states/compare/california-vs-oregon/2025"},{"title":"Oregon Tax Brackets 2026","url":"https://ustax.tools/oregon-tax-brackets-2026/"},{"title":"All comparisons","url":"https://paychecktaxcalculator.net/compare/oregon-vs-california"},{"title":"All comparisons","url":"https://paychecktaxcalculator.net/compare/california-vs-oregon"},{"title":"State Income Tax Comparison","url":"https://usasymbol.com/compare/california-vs-oregon/income-tax"}]

For 2025, California's top state rate is 13.3% and Oregon's is 9.9%, so Oregon's top rate is 3.4 points lower.

- **California:** The 13.3% rate applies only to income above $1,000,000. Ten brackets run from 1% up, per the 2025 bracket table on brackets.tax.
- **Oregon:** The 9.9% rate starts at $125,000 for single filers, a threshold that is unusually low compared with other states. Oregon has four brackets, starting at 4.75%, per the 2025 comparison on brackets.tax.

Because California's top rate applies only at much higher incomes, it is far less significant for most earners. One source notes that California's progressive brackets mean your effective rate is much lower than 13.3% for most earners. At a $100,000 salary, the 2025 figures show California is about $2,984 cheaper, though the sources differ on the exact dollar gap. The 2026 comparison sites put Oregon ahead at that income, so the result depends on the year and the calculator.

Sources note that bracket thresholds can change from year to year, so check the official FTB and Oregon DOR figures before relying on these numbers.

Links: [{"title":"What's The Average Rent In Portland, OR - 2026","url":"https://www.steadily.com/blog/average-rent-portland"},{"title":"san francisco ca vs portland or","url":"https://movenumbers.com/compare/san-francisco-ca-vs-portland-or"},{"title":"portland or vs san francisco ca","url":"https://movenumbers.com/compare/portland-or-vs-san-francisco-ca"},{"title":"50 Cities Where the Cost of Living Is Out of Control","url":"https://www.aol.com/50-cities-where-cost-living-114131601.html"},{"title":"digital release.koin","url":"https://digital-release.koin.com/?p=1074020"},{"title":"What is the real cost of living in Portland, OR?","url":"https://bungalow.com/articles/what-is-the-real-cost-of-living-in-portland-or"},{"title":"portland vs san francisco","url":"https://affordwhere.com/compare/portland-vs-san-francisco"},{"title":"How Portland's cost of living stacks up along the West coast","url":"https://www.axios.com/local/portland/2023/11/14/cost-of-living-portland-oregon-home-transportation-food-prices"},{"title":"Digital Database","url":"https://new.risingsunartscentre.org/news/cost-of-living-in-portland-oregon-price-insights-for-20262025.html"}]

The search turned up no single authoritative 2025 rent index comparing the two areas directly. The sources are mostly comparison calculators and older studies, and they don't fully agree.

- **Calculator comparisons:** MoveNumbers puts San Francisco's overall cost index well above Portland's, with its figures dated 2026. Its two pages use different base cities, so the percentage gap flips depending on which direction you check. One shows Portland about 34% cheaper, the other shows San Francisco about 51.5% more expensive. Its calculator estimates monthly savings of about $2.6K for a move to Portland from San Francisco, and its rent figures come from HUD ZIP-level estimates.
- **Rent ranges:** On AffordWhere, 1-bedroom rents in Portland range from $1,340 to $2,360 per month across 3 neighborhoods, while in San Francisco they range from $2,400 to $4,600 across 9 neighborhoods. Its overall verdict is that Portland is generally cheaper to live in across rent, groceries, transport, and dining, though costs vary by neighborhood and lifestyle.
- **Portland average rent:** Steadily reports that the average rent in Portland, OR, is $1,860 per month as of September 2025, with a one-bedroom averaging about $1,550.
- **Axios (2023):** Axios found that compared to California cities of more than 100,000 residents, Portland came in as less expensive than San Jose, San Francisco, Los Angeles, San Diego and Oakland. This is older data.
- **Salary needed:** SmartAsset's ranking placed the San Francisco Bay Area at the top spot for the highest salary needed to live comfortably, with Portland-Vancouver-Hillsboro coming in at No. 8.

Overall, the sources agree that Portland is substantially cheaper than the Bay Area, mainly on housing. The exact size of the gap depends on the source and the year. For a precise 2025 rent index, check the HUD Fair Market Rents or Zillow/Apartment List city reports directly.

Links: [{"title":"sdi tax","url":"https://www.keka.com/us/glossary/sdi-tax"},{"title":"California State Disability Insurance: How the 2025 Rate Change Impacts Businesses and Employees","url":"https://www.onedigital.com/en-US/articles/ca-sdi-changes-removal-of-wage-ceiling-set-to-impact-employers-and-employees-in-2024/"},{"title":"ca sdi tax 2025 what californians need to know about paycheck deductions and benefits","url":"https://ai.joinwarp.com/ca-sdi-tax-2025-what-californians-need-to-know-about-paycheck-deductions-and-benefits"},{"title":"SDI Tax: Meaning, Eligibility, Rates & Calculation [2025] | Keka HR","url":"https://www.keka.com/glossary/sdi-tax"},{"title":"California State Disability Insurance: How the 2025 Rate Change Impacts Businesses and Employees","url":"https://www.onedigital.com/blog/ca-sdi-changes-removal-of-wage-ceiling-set-to-impact-employers-and-employees-in-2024"},{"title":"new year brings higher taxes on california employees and employers deja vu all over again","url":"https://caltax.org/2025/01/06/new-year-brings-higher-taxes-on-california-employees-and-employers-deja-vu-all-over-again/"},{"title":"2025 Federal Social Security, California SDI Taxable Wage Base, Withholding Rates","url":"https://hrwatchdog.calchamber.com/?p=17170"},{"title":"new year brings higher taxes on california employees and employers deja vu all over again","url":"https://caltax.org/new-year-brings-higher-taxes-on-california-employees-and-employers-deja-vu-all-over-again"},{"title":"edd.ca.gov","url":"https://EDD.ca.gov/siteassets/files/disability/pdf/edddiforecastjan24.pdf"},{"title":"Contribution Rates, Withholding Schedules, and Meals and Lodging Values","url":"https://edd.ca.gov/en/Payroll_taxes/Rates_and_withholding"}]

The search results agree that California's 2025 SDI rate is 1.2% and that there is no wage cap.

- **Rate:** The EDD's official rates page states the 2025 withholding rate is 1.2 percent (The SDI withholding rate for 2025 is 1.2 percent.). A CalChamber summary gives the same figure, up from 1.1% in 2024 (For 2025, the SDI withholding rate for employees is 1.2 percent, compared with 1.1 percent in 2024.). One Keka page lists 1.1% for 2025 in one spot, but its own table and other sources give 1.2%, so that appears to be an error.
- **Wage cap:** SB 951 removed the cap starting January 1, 2024. The EDD notes that Senate Bill 951 removes the taxable wage limit and maximum withholdings for each employee subject to SDI contributions. The last cap was $153,164 in 2023 (the taxable wage cap ($153,164 in 2023) was eliminated as a result of SB 951).
- **Practical effect:** Because the cap is gone, the 1.2% applies to all covered wages, including bonuses and commissions. For example, a $170,000 earner would owe about $2,040 in 2025 (The same employee earning the same amount in 2025 will pay $2,040 ($170,000 x 1.2 percent) in SDI.).
- **Rate changes:** The rate is set annually and can move. Statute keeps it between 0.1% and 1.5% (the rate may not exceed 1.5 percent or be less than 0.1 percent).

Employers should confirm the current year's rate on the EDD site before running payroll, since the 2026 rate is not in these results.

Co. commissioners accused of 'kicking the can' after vote on free preschool program","url":"https://www.katu.com/news/local/mult-co-commissioners-accused-of-kicking-the-can-after-vote-on-free-preschool-program-for-all-julie-brim-edwards-jessica-vega-pederson"},{"title":"ILWU Payroll Bulletin SHS and Preschool Tax","url":"https://pmanet.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/ILWU_Payroll_Bulletin_SHS_and_Preschool_Tax.pdf"},{"title":"City Cast Portland logo","url":"https://portland.citycast.fm/explainers/portland-area-local-income-taxes-explained"},{"title":"Multnomah County Preschool For All Personal Income Tax","url":"https://multco.us/node/85310"},{"title":"Multnomah County Universal Preschool Initiative Coming to the Ballot","url":"https://aldrichadvisors.com/?p=30093"},{"title":"Employee Notification 1","url":"https://cdn.wou.edu/hr/files/2022/02/Employee-Notification-1.pdf"},{"title":"portland oregon tax guide 2026","url":"https://www.countrytaxcalc.com/tax-guides/usa/portland-oregon-tax-guide-2026/"}]

Here's what the search found for 2025 (current as of the latest sources, which are from late 2025 or 2026):

**Preschool for All (PFA), Multnomah County:** The tax is 1.5% on Multnomah County taxable income above $125,000 for single filers or $200,000 for joint filers, plus an additional 1.5% above $250,000 (single) or $400,000 (joint). The personal income tax rate is 1.5% on Multnomah County taxable income over $125,000 for individuals or $200,000 for joint filers, and an additional 1.5% on Multnomah County taxable income over $250,000 for individuals or $400,000 for joint filers. The county's FAQ, revised October 6, 2025, confirms these thresholds. The tax is due by April 15th the following year.

**Rate increase timing (conflicting sources):** The city and county say the rate rises by 0.8% in 2027. Beginning January 1, 2027, there will be a rate increase of 0.8%. This means the 1.5% rate will increase to 2.3% and the 3% rate will increase to 3.8%. Older material, such as a 2022 university employee notice, said the increase would come in 2026, so that date is outdated.

**Supportive Housing Services (SHS), Metro:** The SHS tax is 1% on income above $125,000 for single filers and $200,000 for joint filers. The SHS program is partially funded by a 1% personal income tax. It applies to residents of the Metro district and to nonresidents with income sourced there. It applies to everyone who lives and works inside the Metro region (within the growth boundary, and not in rural areas; you can check your address if you're not sure).

**Withholding and filing:** Both taxes are administered by the City of Portland Revenue Division. Multnomah County Preschool For All Personal Income Tax and Metro Supportive Housing Services will have separate withholding returns remitted to the City of Portland. Employers automatically withhold PFA tax for employees earning over $200,000 from a single employer, and employees can opt out using a METRO/MultCo form.

Neither San Francisco nor any other California city or county currently levies a local personal income tax on residents. Some search results say otherwise, but they're unreliable.

- **Statewide ban:** California has never allowed local income taxes. In 1963, amid rumblings to enact them, the Legislature passed a law forbidding them. A 2025 San Francisco Board of Supervisors resolution also states that California does not currently allow cities or counties to enact local taxes on income or wealth.
- **San Francisco specifically:** A 2026 tax guide says San Francisco does not impose a local personal income tax — residents only pay California state income tax. Residents pay state income tax, which ranges up to 14.4% for incomes over $1 million per that guide.
- **Pending push for change:** The city has sought permission to tax personal and corporate income. The Board of Supervisors plans to vote next week on a resolution urging the California Legislature to amend state law to allow cities and other local governments to impose personal and corporate income taxes. Changing the law would require the Legislature and the governor, then local voter approval. I did not find confirmation that this has passed.
- **Conflicting sources:** A few pages (nacdashboard.nara.gov and an everycalculators.com 2018 calculator) claim San Francisco charges a 1.5% local income tax on residents. These conflict with the sources above, and I'd treat them as unreliable.

1	<!-- GENERATED — DO NOT EDIT. Source: shared/spine/references/output-template.md. Regenerate via: scripts/sync-content.py --write. -->
2	
3	# First Principles Analysis Output Template
4	
5	> **Note:** This is the full annotated template with complete section guidance, type
6	> definitions, and prescriptions. A condensed skeleton showing just the required section
7	> names and chain format lives resident in the agent body (`SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface) for quick reference. Come here
8	> for the complete instructions when authoring or reviewing an analysis. To read a delivered analysis for business value rather than write one, see `how-to-read.md`, which the agent copies beside the reports as `HOW-TO-READ.md`.
9	
10	## How to Use This Template
11	
12	This template is a **strict-shape document**. All six sections must be present in the fixed order below. No section may be omitted.
13	
14	If a section has no genuine content for a given analysis — because the problem is simple, the domain has no relevant dead ends, or the section truly does not apply — mark it with the honest-depth escape valve:
15	
16	> `Nothing material here — [reason explaining why this section has no content for this particular analysis and that the omission is justified, not lazy]`
17	
18	The section heading must still appear. The escape valve exists to prevent box-ticking fabrication: it is always better to write `Nothing material here — [reason]` than to fill a section with words that say nothing.
19	
20	**Section order (fixed):**
21	1. Problem Essence
22	2. Assumptions Table
23	3. Ground Truths
24	4. Derivation Chains
25	5. Abandoned Reasoning
26	6. Conclusion
27	
28	### Document order
29	
30	The delivered file is not just these six sections — it is assembled in one absolute order: a
31	short `## Answer` block; then sections 1 through 6 above, in the fixed order and unchanged; then
32	one `## Appendix — process output` heading; then every process-output block produced during the
33	run, in the order produced, each keeping its own existing top-level heading, and the structured summary last of all.
34	
35	The `## Answer` block sits above section 1 and carries three bold lead-ins: `**Recommendation:**`
36	(1–3 sentences restating §6's `**Recommended approach:**`), `**Band (from §6):**` (§6's own
37	`**Confidence:**` band, copied verbatim), and `**Would change it:**` (the evidence or verification
38	§6 names as capable of moving the band or the recommendation). Each lead-in cites at least one
39	chain inline — `(chain Cn)` — and every chain it cites is one §6 already cites for the claim being
40	restated: the Answer states nothing §6 does not already state with the same chain. It is at most
41	120 words, is written last from the final §6 text, and is not a seventh output section. Before the
42	file is assembled, each Answer line is confirmed to restate a §6 claim and name its chain; a line
43	that does not is cut, not softened.
44	
45	**The structured summary closes the appendix.** The last process-output block in the file is
46	`## Structured summary (process output)`: that heading, then exactly one fenced `json` block,
47	and nothing after it. The block restates, in the fixed fields
48	`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/summary-schema.json` defines, decisions the six sections and
49	the process-output blocks already record — each assumption's type and verdict, each ground truth
50	and whether it was read at source, each chain's confidence and what it rests on, the dead ends,
51	the techniques applied and declined, every Self-Audit Gate scoring pass in order, whether any
52	re-entry edge fired, and the recommendation in full with its confidence and what it rests on — and it adds none:
53	every id in it is one the document uses and every value agrees with the document. A reader who
54	skips it loses nothing. It is process output, not environment state, and it is not a seventh
55	output section. The agent's final message does not carry it; the block exists only in the
56	delivered file.
57	
58	**Nothing about the environment enters the document.** The six sections above are the whole deliverable, and none of them has a slot for the state of the session that produced it. Tooling, connector, authorisation, permission, quota, configuration, model, harness and transcript state are all environment state, and none of it belongs in the analysis — not in a section, not appended after §6, not as a footnote. This exclusion is about environment-state *content*, never about physical position in the file: the trailing `## Appendix — process output` sits after §6 and carries process output — the Self-Audit Gate's verdict blocks, the closure ledger, the self-audit scan, the adversarial pass record, the structured summary — none of which is environment state, and its presence there does not reopen this rule. The class is *any* fact about the machinery rather than about the problem; it is not a list of forbidden words, and a new kind of environment fact is covered by this rule on the day it first exists. A prefix such as "Unrelated to this analysis", "Separately" or "Note:" does not make such a paragraph admissible — it marks the writer as already knowing the paragraph does not belong, which is the point at which it is dropped rather than labelled. Where environment state genuinely blocked the analysis, it is already disclosed in its proper place: a failed reference read under the template's own disclosure rule, and an unmet evidence need as a `?`-marked input carried into the Assumptions Table and named on the affected `**Confidence:**` line. Environment state that blocked nothing is reported to the user outside the deliverable, after the document ends, or not at all.
59	
60	---
61	
62	## 1. Problem Essence
63	
64	State the core problem in a single sentence — not the symptoms, not the solution space, but the irreducible question the analysis must answer.
65	
66	**Core problem:** [One sentence. Strip away implementation details and surface the underlying question.]
67	
68	**Success criteria:** [Measurable, observable outcomes that would confirm the problem is solved. A skeptic must be able to verify these without asking for further clarification.]
69	
70	---
71	
72	## 2. Assumptions Table
73	
74	List every assumption — explicit and implicit — that the analysis rests on. Classify each by type and apply the prescribed treatment. An assumption omitted from this table is an assumption that will propagate unchallenged through every later step.
75	
76	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
77	|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
78	| [Assumption text] | [physical law / current constraint / convention / untested belief] | [prescribed action per type — see below] | [Accept / Challenge / Discard] — [justification/reason] | [source, or "unverified — flagged" if used in a chain per D-07] |
79	
80	**These five columns are the whole table — no ID column.** Assumptions are referred to by the
81	`[Assumes: A-N]` marks the chains carry and by the `A-N` labels used in the Assumption Audit
82	scan; adding a sixth ID column to this table duplicates that identity in a second place, and two
83	places that name the same thing drift. A run that adds one is deviating from this template even
84	though nothing rejects it today.
85	
86	### Type Definitions and Prescribed Treatments
87	
88	**physical law** — a constraint imposed by physics, mathematics, or formal logic that cannot change regardless of context or decisions made.
89	Prescribed treatment: accept as a ground-truth candidate and record it in the Ground Truths section.
90	
91	**current constraint** — a real limitation that applies now but could change (budget, team size, regulatory environment, technology availability).
92	Prescribed treatment: record the expiry conditions — what would have to change for this constraint to no longer hold. Do not treat it as permanent.
93	
94	**convention** — a practice or standard that exists because it has been adopted, not because it is physically or logically required.
95	Prescribed treatment: explicitly challenge the convention before accepting it. "We do it this way" is not a justification.
96	
97	**untested belief** — a claim held as true that has not been empirically verified in the context of this analysis.
98	Prescribed treatment: verify it, or flag it unverified. An untested belief used in a derivation chain must be marked with the `GT-N?` notation (see Ground Truths) and any conclusion depending on it inherits a confidence caveat.
99	
100	### Stakes-Escalation Rule
101	
102	The higher the stakes of the conclusion resting on an assumption, the more that assumption must be pushed toward physical law or verified ground truth status. Classification drives the method — it does not merely label.
103	
104	### Verdict Vocabulary
105	
106	The Verdict cell is a token prefix followed by an em-dash and the justification — the bare
107	token leads so it stays matchable, and the em-dash prose carries the reasoning. **The separator
108	is an em-dash, never a colon.** `Accept: the figure is audited` puts the token and the reasoning
109	on one side of a punctuation mark that appears throughout ordinary prose, so the cell stops being
110	matchable — which is the whole property the token-first form exists to provide. Measured: a single
111	run using the colon form scored ten non-conforming verdict cells at once. The em-dash is not a
112	stylistic preference here; it is the delimiter:
113	
114	- **Accept** — the assumption survives challenge and may be used in the analysis (e.g., "Accept — survives P2 challenge; physical-law backed by GT-1")
115	- **Challenge** — the assumption is questionable; probe further before use (e.g., "Challenge — vendor benchmark unverified, flagged GT-5?")
116	- **Discard** — the assumption is false or irrelevant; remove from the reasoning chain (e.g., "Discard — contradicted by GT-2, no longer load-bearing")
117	
118	**A current-constraint verdict records its expiry at the point of use.** An assumption classified `current constraint` is accepted only until that constraint lapses; the verdict cell says when. The expiry belongs in the em-dash justification and never in the token slot — the token slot carries one of the three tokens above and nothing else.
119	
120	**Conforming — a current constraint recording its expiry:**
121	
122	```text
123	Accept — expires at term end (1 or 3 years); until then the constraint is contractual, not physical
124	```
125	
126	**Non-conforming — the expiry hoisted into the token slot:**
127	
128	```text
129	Current constraint (expires at term end) — contractual, not physical
130	```
131	
132	The vocabulary above is unchanged because run 3 rendered four current-constraint rows conformingly on the identical prompt by putting the expiry in the justification — this is a worked example, not a schema change.
133	
134	---
135	
136	## 3. Ground Truths
137	
138	List the irreducible, verified facts the analysis builds on. Each ground truth carries a stable identifier used by the Derivation Chains section. Once assigned, an ID does not change.
139	
140	A ground truth must pass this test: it is a fact that is true regardless of what solution is chosen, verifiable independently of the analysis, and not derived from another item on this list.
141	
142	Every ground truth carries a **provenance label** answering one question: *did this analysis read the asserted figure or wording in the cited source?* The answer decides the suffix. A citation being present is not verification — a citation can name a real document and be wrong about what is in it.
143	
144	**Verified ground truth form** (provenance `read-at-source` — no suffix):
145	
146	- **GT-1** [fact text] — source: [verification source — data, measurement, published spec, direct observation]; read-at-source: [page, table, section, or quoted passage where the figure was read]
147	- **GT-2** [fact text] — source: [verification source]; read-at-source: [where read]
148	
149	**Delegate-reported ground truth form** (provenance `reported-by-delegate` — `?` required):
150	
151	- **GT-3?** [fact text] — cited to: [source the delegate named]; reported-by-delegate: [which sub-agent, search, or summary supplied it] — cited source not opened by this analysis
152	
153	**Unverified ground truth form (D-07)** (provenance `unverified` — `?` required):
154	
155	- **GT-4?** [fact text] — unverified: [specific reason the fact could not be verified in this analysis]
156	
157	The `?` suffix signals that this ground truth has not been read at its source — whether because it is an untested belief or because a delegate reported it and nobody opened the citation. Any conclusion depending on a `GT-N?` input inherits a confidence caveat in the Derivation Chains section. The analysis may proceed with such inputs — but the uncertainty must be visible.
158	
159	**The `?` is the default.** Drop it only when the read-at-source location can be named. A delegate report counts as read-at-source only when it quotes the source's own wording and that quote was checked — not when it merely supplies a well-formed citation.
160	
161	**Provenance summary (required):** enumerate the `?`-marked ground truths **by ID**, and for every unsuffixed ground truth feeding a load-bearing chain — one a conclusion this analysis presents rests on, whatever its band — name its read-at-source location. This is the same population the Phase 3 exit criterion names: scoping it to HIGH chains would let an unread figure excuse itself, because the `?` it takes caps its chain below HIGH. Write the list, not a number:
162	
163	```text
164	?-marked: GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14 (4 of 22)
165	Read-at-source: GT-3 — 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)(i), subsections (A)/(B)/(R) quoted verbatim
166	```
167	
168	A stated integer does not satisfy this — an integer cannot be checked against the list it summarizes, and an enumeration can. Where a count and its enumeration disagree, **the enumeration governs.** Neither an empty enumeration nor a count of zero satisfies this on its own; the named locations are the auditable part.
169	
170	IDs are stable once assigned. GT-3 remains GT-3 throughout the document even if GT-3 is later verified or discarded.
171	
172	---
173	
174	## 4. Derivation Chains
175	
176	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
177	
178	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
179	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
180	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
181	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
182	
183	**Chain format:**
184	
185	```text
186	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
187	```
188	
189	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
190	
191	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
192	
193	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
194	
195	```text
196	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
197	→ [intermediate claim]
198	→ [further intermediate]
199	→ [conclusion]
200	```
201	
202	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
203	
204	```text
205	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
206	→ [intermediate claim]
207	→ [conclusion]
208	```
209	
210	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
211	
212	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
213	
214	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
215	
216	```text
217	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
218	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
219	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
220	```
221	
222	**Non-conforming — a hop broken across physical lines:**
223	
224	```text
225	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
226	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
227	  once idle-time billing is included
228	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate
229	```
230	
231	The continuation line does not begin with `→`, so the chain terminates at the head's first hop and what remains reads as an incomplete chain.
232	
233	**Non-conforming — the same hops rendered as a numbered list:**
234	
235	```text
236	1. GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
237	2. Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute
238	3. sustained workloads belong on Fargate
239	```
240	
241	A numbered list restates each hop as its own GT-headed one-hop chain, which reads as several incomplete chains rather than one complete one — the intermediate steps stop being connected to the conclusion they build toward.
242	
243	**Non-conforming — an input carrying unparenthesized prose:**
244	
245	```text
246	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2's threshold
247	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
248	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
249	```
250	
251	`C2's threshold` is not an identifier — it is a possessive prose phrase — so the head does not parse; the third input must be written `C2 (threshold)`.
252	
253	**Conforming — the same head with the upstream chain as an input:**
254	
255	```text
256	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown) + C2 (threshold)
257	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
258	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
259	```
260	
261	Exactly one token differs from the block above: a `Cn` identifier with a parenthesized gloss is an admissible head input, on equal footing with a `GT-N` identifier.
262	
263	**Conforming — a chain consuming only upstream conclusions:**
264	
265	```text
266	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold) + C4 (unconditional, zero code change) + C5 (~73% ceiling, no execution-model change)
267	→ C4 and C5 deliver verified savings that do not depend on any property of your workload
268	→ C2's saving depends entirely on a duty-cycle figure nobody has measured
269	```
270	
271	A head may consist entirely of `Cn` inputs with no `GT-N` term. The second hop's `C2's saving` is prose, not a head input — the head-only scope note is what permits it here.
272	
273	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same prose input in a non-final position:**
274	
275	```text
276	GT-13? (bill composition unknown) + C2's threshold + GT-12? (duty cycle unknown)
277	→ target quantity: fraction of total AWS bill removed by the migration
278	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
279	```
280	
281	This head breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with a well-formed input still to its right the check matches from `GT-12?` onward and never reaches `C2's threshold`. Write `C2 (threshold)` wherever the input sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
282	
283	**Non-conforming — a hop beginning with a GT-N identifier:**
284	
285	```text
286	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
287	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
288	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
289	```
290	
291	The second line reads as the head of a new chain because it begins with a `GT-N` identifier, so this chain ends after its head and what remains is an incomplete chain — the possessive is not the problem, the leading identifier is.
292	
293	**Conforming — the same hop with the identifier moved off the front:**
294	
295	```text
296	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
297	→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates
298	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
299	```
300	
301	Exactly one clause is reordered and the chain is whole again; naming a ground truth inside a hop is fine, leading with its identifier is not.
302	
303	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the GT-led hop in a later position:**
304	
305	```text
306	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
307	→ the bracket straddles zero, so its two ends recommend opposite actions
308	→ the second reading is the binding one
309	→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term in both estimates
310	```
311	
312	This hop breaks the same rule as the non-conforming block above and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — the check has already satisfied its two-arrow requirement on the hops that precede it, so the leading identifier ends the chain there without changing the verdict. Write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term in both estimates` wherever the hop sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
313	
314	**Non-conforming — the first hop closing its own sentence:**
315	
316	```text
317	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
318	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape.
319	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
320	```
321	
322	This chain violates none of R1-R9 — every input parses, every hop states one inference, no hop leads with a `GT-N` identifier — and is scored malformed anyway, because the mechanical form check ends the chain the moment the first hop closes its own sentence, before its two-arrow requirement is satisfied, and never reaches the well-formed hop that follows.
323	
324	**Conforming — the same chain with the first hop's terminal period removed:**
325	
326	```text
327	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
328	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
329	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes
330	```
331	
332	Exactly one character differs from the block above: the terminal period. Removing it, and nothing else, restores the two-arrow match the check requires.
333	
334	**Non-conforming, and undetected by the form check — the same period moved to a later hop:**
335	
336	```text
337	C1 (2.20× at full duty) + C2 (conditional on an unmeasured threshold)
338	→ C1's saving is unconditional and does not depend on workload shape
339	→ the migration case does not rest on C1 alone
340	→ C2's saving is real only above the duty-cycle threshold this estimate assumes.
341	```
342	
343	This block breaks the identical rule one hop later and is equally non-conforming, but the mechanical form check scores it conforming — with two hops already matched before the closing sentence is reached, the check has satisfied its two-arrow requirement and the sentence-closing period on the third hop has no following line left to block. Write the closing hop with no terminal punctuation wherever it sits; the rule is the contract, and the check is a partial instrument for it.
344	
345	**One-inference rule.** A hop states exactly ONE inference. If a hop joins two claims with "and", or carries a parenthetical that could stand as its own claim, it is two hops — split it.
346	
347	TELL (not the rule): a hop past ~200 characters is almost always two hops. Measure the hop, then split — do not wrap it, and do not trim words to hit a number.
348	
349	Inline annotations (`*[Assumes: A14 — …]*`) attach to the end of the hop line they qualify and do not start a new hop.
350	
351	### Converting structured-technique outputs into chains
352	
353	Structured-technique outputs (trade-off matrices, second-order effect lists) do not appear in this section as-is — each converts into the chain format above using the rule for its technique below. This subsection is the single source of truth for the conversion; the per-technique Handoff sections point back here rather than restating it, so future structured techniques extend this one place.
354	
355	**Trade-off matrix → one chain.** A trade-off matrix collapses into ONE chain whose intermediate cites the winning weighted total and whose endpoint names a single recommended option:
356	
357	```text
358	GT-refs (criteria's factual basis) → weighted totals (the winning total vs. the runner-up, naming the high-weight criteria that drive it) → recommended option
359	```
360	
361	Example: `GT-2 + GT-5 (criteria facts) → weighted totals: B=82 > A=64, driven by reliability×warranty → recommend B`. The full matrix stays in the technique's own output — this subsection carries only the single collapsed chain, never the matrix re-expressed row-by-row (that would violate the one-chain-per-conclusion rule above). An exact tie between weighted totals still resolves to a single named recommended option; a tie must not produce a multi-option chain endpoint. **Exact-tie tiebreak (deterministic):** on an exact tie, prefer the option with fewer `GT-N?` (unverified) inputs among its winning criteria; if still tied, name both totals in the chain intermediate but select the first-listed option as the chain endpoint, and flag the tie explicitly in the Conclusion section's confidence line.
362	
363	**Second-order effect list → order-marked extension.** A second-order effect list extends the parent chain IN PLACE as additional order-marked steps, each carrying the same evidentiary discipline as the first-order steps that produced the conclusion:
364	
365	```text
366	GT-N → first-order conclusion →[2nd] [2nd-order effect] →[3rd] [3rd-order effect] (contradicts GT-M → back to Phase 2)
367	```
368	
369	Example: `GT-1 → first-order conclusion →[2nd] flag-config surface grows →[3rd] flag debt accumulates (contradicts GT-4 → back to P2)`. The order marks (`[2nd]`, `[3rd]`) make the extension's sequence legible. A contradicting effect routes the conclusion back to Phase 2 — never directly to Phase 3 or past Phase 2. A pass that surfaces no non-contradicting downstream effect leaves the parent chain unextended — a clean no-op, not an error.
370	
371	### Confidence levels, defined
372	
373	`HIGH`, `MEDIUM` and `LOW` name how much of a chain is **outstanding** — not how strongly the analysis believes its conclusion. Three axes decide the band, each answerable by inspecting what the chain already carries on the page:
374	
375	- **Inputs** — the provenance of every identifier on the head line: an unsuffixed `GT-N` with a named read-at-source location, a `?`-marked ground truth, or a `Cn` carrying its own band.
376	- **Inference** — whether each hop the chain's endpoint depends on follows from the line above it, or needs a premise supplied by an `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation.
377	- **Rivals** — whether a competing conclusion from the same ground truths survives, and what rules it out. Section 5 is where the ruling-out is written down, so a chain answers this axis by pointing at its own Abandoned Reasoning entry as readily as by carrying the rival on its confidence line.
378	
379	**The band is the lowest the three axes license.** A chain is not HIGH because two of them are clean.
380	
381	**HIGH — nothing on this chain is outstanding.** Every identifier on the head line is an unsuffixed `GT-N` whose read-at-source location is named, or a `Cn` itself rated HIGH; every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity cited to an unsuffixed ground truth; and the strongest rival conclusion the analysis considered is named — on this confidence line or in a section 5 entry this chain points to — together with the ground truth or chain that rules it out, that ruling-out input itself unsuffixed. A chain whose endpoint a live alternative still contests is unexamined, not certain: it is MEDIUM at best.
382	
383	An `[Assumes: A-N]` annotation on a hop shorts the Inference axis **unless** the confidence line says what becomes of the endpoint when that assumption fails and the endpoint still stands — *"A2 is that the CDN'd assets are versioned; if they were not, the CDN result would be weaker evidence still, so the conclusion is unaffected"*. An annotation on a hop that only qualifies a second-order extension, and not the endpoint, is outside this axis and the chain says which case it is. Stating the sensitivity is the work; an unexamined assumption is not the same thing as one whose falsity has been priced.
384	
385	The Rivals axis is answered when a section 5 entry names a competing conclusion to this chain's endpoint and the chain or ground truth that ruled it out, or when the endpoint is itself a ruling-out — a chain establishing that some option does not work has already done the rival's work and does not need a rival of its own. It is short when a competing conclusion has been raised anywhere in the analysis and nothing settles it, and when the analysis reaches a positive recommendation with no section 5 content bearing on it at all.
386	
387	**MEDIUM — exactly one axis is short, and the shortfall is named and bounded.** One of: an identifier on the head line is `?`-marked or is a `Cn` rated MEDIUM; or at most one hop the endpoint depends on rests on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise whose failure the chain has not priced; or a rival to the endpoint is live and nothing in the analysis settles it. The confidence line names which axis is short, names the specific input, hop or rival, and states what would close it — the verification that would remove an input as a cause of the downgrade, the evidence that would establish an assumed premise, or the observation that would settle between this conclusion and its rival. A MEDIUM chain is one whose weakness a reader can point at.
388	
389	**LOW — the shortfall is unbounded, or more than one axis is short.** Two or more axes short at once; or an input is `?` with no verification path available; or a hop's missing premise cannot be stated as an assumption at all, so the analysis cannot say what would make the step valid; or a rival survives that no available observation would settle. A LOW chain is reportable, and a conclusion resting on it alone is not actionable.
390	
391	**Calibration rule.** Each rating is the highest its inputs, hops and rivals license, **and no higher**. Rating above what the axes license over-claims. Rating below it is a defect of the same kind: a chain meeting HIGH on all three axes and written MEDIUM misreports the analysis's own strength, and a document whose every chain carries the same defensive band tells a reader nothing about which parts to trust. Criterion 5 scores calibration, not altitude — an analysis whose every band is the one its axes license is Rigorous whether its conclusion is HIGH, MEDIUM or LOW.
392	
393	**The caps are consequences, not extra rules.** The unverified-input rule (D-07) below and the ceiling at the lowest-rated chain a head cites are what the Inputs axis says, restated for the two cases that occur most often; they are the fast check, and these definitions are what they check for. A cap never licenses a band on its own — it bounds from above, and the band is still the lowest any of the three axes licenses.
394	
395	**Confidence pre-check (Inputs axis).** Directly above every `**Confidence:**` line — each §4 chain's and the §6 Conclusion's — write one `**Pre-check:**` line, with nothing between it and the `**Confidence:**` line it checks:
396	
397	```text
398	**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-3?, C2 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-3? · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
399	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-3? is unverified; …
400	```
401	
402	Four fields, separated by ` · `: `head` lists every identifier on the chain's head line (the part before the first `→`), in order, comma-separated, a `?` suffix kept (`GT-3?`), each `Cn` followed by its own stated band in parentheses (`C2 (MEDIUM)`) — for the §6 roll-up, `head` is every chain the Conclusion rests on, each with its band, plus any `GT-N?` the Conclusion rests on directly. `?-marked` lists the `?`-suffixed identifiers from `head`, comma-separated, or the token `none`. `lowest cited` is the lowest band among the `Cn` in `head`, or `none` when `head` cites no chain. `Inputs ceiling` is the Inputs axis's bound: `LOW` if `lowest cited` is LOW; otherwise `MEDIUM` if `?-marked` is not `none` or `lowest cited` is MEDIUM; otherwise `HIGH`.
403	
404	This is the Inputs axis of "Confidence levels, defined" made procedural — Inference and Rivals are not scored on this line, and can only lower the band further. The ceiling bounds from above, as the caps-are-consequences paragraph above states; the `**Confidence:**` label may equal it or sit below it, and never above it — a below-ceiling label is explained by the Confidence line itself, not by the pre-check. In §6, the pre-check line is itself a Conclusion-section claim under the Claim inventory rule below, and it is cited by the chains its own `head` names.
405	
406	### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]
407	
408	GT-N ([brief fact label, source]) + GT-M ([brief fact label, source])
409	→ [intermediate claim — a new inference statable from combining GT-N and GT-M but from neither alone]
410	→ [conclusion — the claim this chain establishes]
411	
412	**Pre-check:** head [every head identifier; each Cn with its band, e.g. C2 (MEDIUM)] · ?-marked: [the GT-N? identifiers, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest Cn band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
413	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
414	[If MEDIUM or LOW: name each GT-N? input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; name each Cn on this chain's head rated below HIGH, which need not be re-explained here; and give each downgrade cause belonging to this chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists (the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause).]
415	
416	**Unverified input rule (D-07):** A chain that includes any `GT-N?` input must end with a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line. The line must name the unverified input and state the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. A HIGH confidence claim cannot rest on an unverified ground truth. A chain is also rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites — the stated confidence label of each `Cn` on its head line, the part before the first `→`. This is a ceiling: it bounds the rating from above and is never a reason to rate a chain HIGH, and a cited chain rated MEDIUM under a validation-rubric EXCEPT clause still caps every chain that cites it. Every MEDIUM or LOW confidence line explains only its own chain's rating, so its validity never depends on how far away a cap originates. The line names each `GT-N?` input with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. It names each `Cn` on the chain's head rated below HIGH and need not re-explain that `Cn`, whose own confidence line carries the explanation, so no line has to trace a cited chain's lineage. For each downgrade cause belonging to the chain itself — for example a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation — the line states what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists. A stated reason is the validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause, for an absent-fails derivation, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that cause; "speculative" is never such a reason. The validation-rubric absent-fails EXCEPT clause is the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, and naming any other clause, including the speculative EXCEPT clause, stands in for nothing. A chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing, so the rubric's speculative EXCEPT clause no longer covers it, and the cited chain's own confidence line states its verification path; a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another chain's head, and stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (§5).
417	
418	---
419	
420	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
421	
422	Record every reasoning path that was explored and discarded. This section is required in every analysis. Dead ends are not failures — they are part of the reasoning record and save future analysts from re-exploring paths that have already been ruled out.
423	
424	### Dead End: [Name of discarded path]
425	
426	**What was tried:** [Brief description of the reasoning path that was pursued.]
427	
428	**Why abandoned:** [The specific failure — assumption false, contradicts a ground truth, assumption classification too weak to anchor the chain, conclusion circular, intermediate could not be established, speculative with no verification path (so not cited on another chain's head), etc. Be precise: "we ran out of time" is not a valid abandonment reason.]
429	
430	**What it ruled out:** [What this dead end saves the reader from re-exploring. A well-documented dead end is as valuable as a live conclusion.]
431	
432	If no reasoning was abandoned, write:
433	
434	`Nothing material here — all reasoning paths pursued led to the conclusion above. [Optional: describe the problem's constraint space that made alternative paths infeasible.]`
435	
436	The escape valve still satisfies D-03. Do not omit the heading.
437	
438	---
439	
440	## 6. Conclusion
441	
442	Summarize the analysis result. The Conclusion section synthesizes what the Derivation Chains established — it does not introduce new claims or reasoning.
443	
444	**Recommended approach:** [Description of the recommended course of action, decision, or design choice.]
445	
446	**Key insight:** [The non-obvious finding the first-principles analysis revealed — what reasoning by analogy or convention would have missed.]
447	
448	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** [What is being accepted, deprioritized, or deferred as a result of this recommendation. No recommendation is free of trade-offs.]
449	
450	**Pre-check:** head [each chain the Conclusion rests on with its band, e.g. C1 (MEDIUM), C3 (HIGH); plus any GT-N? it rests on directly] · ?-marked: [ids, or none] · lowest cited: [lowest band, or none] · Inputs ceiling: [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
451	**Confidence:** [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW]
452	
453	If Confidence is MEDIUM or LOW: name each chain contributing to the Conclusion that is rated below HIGH, and each `GT-N?` input the Conclusion rests on directly with the verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade. The line need not restate a named chain's verification path or no-path reason; the named chain's own §4 confidence line carries it. Give any downgrade cause belonging to the Conclusion itself with what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path exists, as §4 defines. A MEDIUM or LOW conclusion without this explanation does not satisfy D-07.
454	
455	**Claim inventory.** A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Three bounds are measured, not assumed: a bold lead-in whose colon-terminated span is the entire physical line and carries no citation of its own is a section-intro label, and the citation obligation then falls to the list items beneath it; a bold span whose closing `**` is not immediately preceded by the colon is not matched at all — write `**Label:** text` to match, not `**Label: text**`; and a list item counts only when it closes its own sentence or runs past forty characters. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
456	
457	**Citation form.** Every Conclusion-section claim either names the chain that established it inline — `(chain C1)` — or is discharged by a §6→§4 closure ledger row that quotes the claim and names its chain. A claim doing neither is cut, not softened. Ledger discharge requires the structural row form the closure-ledger example below shows — a list marker, then the quoted claim, then an arrow, then the chain id — and a prose sentence that merely quotes something and names a chain is not a ledger row. This is detected only when the row sits inside section 6: the ledger emitted as process output in the appendix after section 6 is not visible to the check, and inline citation is therefore the mechanically checkable form.
458	
459	**Conforming — inline chain citation:**
460	
461	```text
462	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate (chain C1).
463	```
464	
465	**Conforming — closure-ledger row:**
466	
467	```text
468	- "Move sustained workloads to Fargate" → chain C1 ✓
469	```
470	
471	**Non-conforming — a claim naming no chain and quoted by no ledger row:**
472	
473	```text
474	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate.
475	```
476	
477	Both forms are accepted because both discharge the same obligation: the ledger is process output emitted in the appendix after section 6 (see the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions"), not a seventh output section, and the chain IDs cited are the `C1`/`C2` IDs assigned by §4's chain-numbering convention.
478	
479	**Caveats.** A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
480	
481	**Not a claim — a bold lead-in alone on its line, carrying no citation:**
482	
483	```text
484	**Recommended approach — three steps, in this order:**
485	```
486	
487	This is the hinge of "detectable from the emission alone" — an author can dodge extraction by putting the lead-in on its own line, and the claim obligation then falls to the numbered items beneath it.
488	
489	**A claim — the same lead-in carrying its assertion on the same line:**
490	
491	```text
492	**Recommended approach:** Move sustained workloads to Fargate before evaluating Lambda (chain C1).
493	```
494	
495	Nothing follows the closing `**` in the block above and something does here, which is the whole difference.
496	
497	**A claim — the lead-in alone on its line, but carrying its own citation:**
498	
499	```text
500	**Recommended approach, established in chain C1:**
501	```
502	
503	The section-intro-label exclusion is conditional on carrying no citation; naming the chain inside the label keeps it a claim.
504	
505	**Not matched at all — a bold span whose colon sits inside it:**
506	
507	```text
508	**Overall confidence: HIGH.**
509	```
510	
511	The extractor requires the colon to close the bold span, so this line is not a claim and not a non-claim — it is never looked at.
512	
513	**A claim — the same statement with the colon closing the bold span:**
514	
515	```text
516	**Overall confidence:** HIGH — seven of eight chains rest on figures read at source (chain C1).
517	```
518	
519	One character moved, and the statement enters the inventory.
520	
521	**Not a claim — a short list item with no sentence-ending punctuation:**
522	
523	```text
524	- Measure duty cycle first
525	```
526	
527	Twenty-four characters and no terminal punctuation, so it falls under the assertiveness floor.
528	
529	**A claim — a short list item closing its own sentence:**
530	
531	```text
532	- Size the Savings Plan after cleanup.
533	```
534	
535	Also under forty characters, so the terminal punctuation is the only thing carrying it over the floor. The two items above are worded differently only so each block is uniquely locatable by the fixture-extraction guard — a true one-character minimal pair would make one block's text a literal prefix of the other's, which no substring needle can discriminate (the `R-HEAD-PERIOD-*` lesson) — and a later control proves the axis is punctuation by re-scoring each block with its punctuation toggled.
536	
537	**Conformant but still untraced — a caveat carrying the flagged-assumption marker:**
538	
539	```text
540	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** the ~73% figure is a ceiling requiring an all-upfront commitment; the realized figure on a no-upfront plan is materially lower — no chain — flagged assumption only.
541	```
542	
543	The marker satisfies the Caveats rule above and the claim still scores untraced; that is honesty-not-score, not a defect, and it is why the extractor is not taught to recognise the marker.
544	
545	**Conformant and traced — the same caveat citing the chain it qualifies:**
546	
547	```text
548	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** the ~73% figure is a ceiling requiring an all-upfront commitment; the realized figure on a no-upfront plan is materially lower (chain C5).
549	```
550	
551	Naming C5 discharges the claim; the marker discloses it. The two rewrites land on different Criterion 6 bands, and that band is assigned by a model — no gate in this tree checks it.
552

1	<!-- GENERATED — DO NOT EDIT. Source: shared/spine/references/validation-rubric.md. Regenerate via: scripts/sync-content.py --write. -->
2	
3	# Self-Audit Gate
4	
5	> **Scope:** This is the Layer-3 scoring instrument read on demand by the validator-fix-repeat loop
6	> already resident in `SKILL.md`. It scores a completed first-principles analysis against the
7	> six-section output format defined in `references/output-template.md`. The loop instruction
8	> itself — when to apply, what to fix, when to stop — lives in `SKILL.md` under
9	> "Before presenting conclusions" and is **not** repeated here. Come here only to score
10	> an analysis in progress; use `SKILL.md` for the loop procedure and `output-template.md`
11	> for authoring guidance.
12	>
13	> **What this instrument scores:** the structure of *this analysis*. It is not a rubric for the
14	> subject matter. When a request asks for a rubric, scorecard, or grading scheme applied to the
15	> thing being analyzed — an article's argument, a proposal, a design — that is a **separate
16	> deliverable** that belongs in the analysis body. Producing it does not satisfy this gate, and
17	> this gate does not substitute for it. Both must appear. (Historically named the "Validation
18	> Rubric"; renamed because that name collided with subject-matter rubrics and the collision was
19	> observed to cause this gate to be skipped.)
20	
21	## How to Apply This Gate
22	
23	Score the completed analysis against all 6 criteria below. For each criterion, produce exactly
24	one verdict block in the format prescribed in the Verdict Block Format section. An analysis
25	clears this gate only when it satisfies **both** of the following conditions — clearing
26	one condition alone does not constitute a pass:
27	
28	1. **Gate cleared** — no criterion scores Absent.
29	2. **Hand-wavy cap cleared** — at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
30	
31	If either condition is not met, revise the analysis and re-score — bounded to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under `SKILL.md`'s Turn discipline section. After that single pass, any criterion still failing — or newly failing as a result of the revision — is presented as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being re-scored again.
32	
33	**Assumption Audit (verify before scoring)**
34	
35	The scan itself is not performed here — the agent already performed it at the end of Phase 4
36	(`SKILL.md`, "End-of-phase Assumption Audit") before this gate is ever applied. This
37	gate's job is narrower: verify the audit ran and its table is exhaustive, not repeat the
38	scan.
39	
40	Before scoring any criterion, confirm the audit table below is present in the analysis and
41	covers every named derivation chain step from section 4 — one row per chain per step, in
42	order, with no step skipped. Do not proceed to verdict blocks until this is confirmed. `Form conforming?` reads `unreached` where a rule binds at a position the mechanical check cannot reach — a disclosed gap in the check, never a softer `no`, and never to be scored as a conforming block. A row whose `Rule applied` cell explains that the check could not reach a position, while `Form conforming?` still reads `yes`, is scoring the block conforming on a rule it never checked; the verdict belongs in `Form conforming?`. `Band` is copied from the chain's own section-4 confidence label, so a disagreement between scan and chain is visible rather than reconciled silently. `Act attempted?` records whether the run tried to open a cited source for that chain's head inputs, and `Edges fired` which bounded re-entry edges fired for it. A load-bearing chain whose inputs are all `?`-marked and whose `Act attempted?` reads `no` is the shape this criterion most needs surfaced: a conclusion reached without once trying to check it.
43	
44	| Chain | Step | Step Text (brief) | Assumption surfaced? | Added to Table? |
45	|-------|------|-------------------|----------------------|-----------------|
46	| [chain producing conclusion X] | 1 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
47	| [chain producing conclusion X] | 2 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
48	| [chain producing conclusion Y] | 1 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
49	
50	If the table is missing, or any named derivation chain step in section 4 has no corresponding
51	row, the audit did not run exhaustively — this is a Criterion 2 defect (see Criterion 2's
52	descriptors below), not a separate gate. Do not re-perform the scan to fill a missing table;
53	a missing or incomplete table is itself the evidence to score against.
54	
55	**Self-audit scan (verify before scoring)**
56	
57	The scan itself is not performed here — the agent already performed it at Phase 5 emission time (`SKILL.md`, "Before presenting conclusions") before the verdict blocks are written. This gate's job is narrower: verify the scan ran and quote its rows, not repeat the scan and not re-derive its rows.
58	
59	This one scan backs two non-adjacent criteria: Criterion 4 quotes the chain-form table, Criterion 6 quotes the claim-inventory table.
60	
61	Before scoring either criterion, confirm the block `## Self-audit scan (process output)` is present in the analysis; that its chain-form table carries one row per section-4 chain block in order with no block skipped; that its claim-inventory table carries one row per section-6 construct in order with no construct skipped, non-claims included; and that its reconciliation line's counts recount against sections 4 and 6. Do not proceed to verdict blocks until this is confirmed.
62	
63	| Chain | Chain Head (brief) | Form conforming? | Rule applied | Dependency clean? | Band | Act attempted? | Edges fired |
64	|-------|---------------------|-------------------|---------------|--------------------|------|-----------------|-------------|

For those limbs the criterion quotes the analysis text directly; the scan is quoted only where the band is determined by what its columns cover.

75	The §6→§4 closure ledger is not admissible as Criterion 4 or Criterion 6 evidence: it is a drafting artifact that ran before the Fix/Repeat loop, and the scan derives its rows from the emitted text of sections 4 and 6 without consulting it.
76	
77	If the scan block is missing, or a section-4 chain block or a section-6 construct has no corresponding row, the scan did not run exhaustively — say so as an unresolved gap in the affected criterion's verdict block. Do not re-perform the scan to fill a missing table; a missing or incomplete scan is itself the evidence to score against.
78	
79	Verifying the scan is present and internally coherent is not verifying its rows are correct — a row's finding is checked against the analysis text by a reader, and no gate in this tree scores a live run's compliance.
80	
81	**Precedence rule (no double-counting):** A single observable defect can match the
82	descriptor of more than one criterion — for example, an unverified ground truth used in a
83	chain without the `?` suffix is named by Criteria 2, 3, and 5. When this happens, band the
84	defect under the **lowest-numbered criterion** whose descriptor names it, and merely *note*
85	the overlap under the other criteria without lowering their band for the same underlying
86	problem. One real flaw must not independently drag down two or three criteria, because that
87	would let a single defect trip the hand-wavy cap on its own.

91	## Exceptions Summary
92	
93	Three conditions relax the HIGH-confidence requirements introduced into Criteria 3 and 5.
94	This section is a navigation aid, listing them together for quick reference; where its
95	wording differs from the per-criterion clause, the per-criterion clause governs.
96	
97	**(a) Unreachable source** — Criterion 3. A ground truth cites a source the Phase 3
98	verification step could not open; the Phase 3 failure record naming which source and why
99	unreachable is the satisfying evidence; the ground truth may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains.
100	
101	**(b) Speculative chain** — Criterion 5. A chain is explicitly marked speculative and the
102	analysis states the claim it supports is not load-bearing; the mark plus that statement is
103	the satisfying evidence; the chain may remain MEDIUM. Its confidence line still gives each of
104	its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account of why no available
105	evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason. A speculative chain cited on
106	another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer qualifies. A speculative chain with no
107	verification path is therefore not cited on another chain's head; it stays speculative or
108	moves to Abandoned Reasoning.
109	
110	**(c) Absent-fails derivation** — Criterion 5. A chain establishes that a conclusion does not
111	follow from an assumption shown to be false; the named false assumption is the satisfying
112	evidence; the chain may remain MEDIUM.
113	
114	An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one names it in the relevant
115	verdict block and cites the required evidence; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the
116	analysis's behalf.

120	## Scoring Model
121	
122	Score each of the 6 criteria using this shared 4-level scale, applied uniformly across all criteria
123	(highest to lowest):
124	
125	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
126	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
127	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
128	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.
129	
130	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
131	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
132	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
133	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.
134	
135	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
136	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
137	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
138	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.
139	
140	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
141	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading
142	  appears with nothing substantive below it).
143	
144	**Rank order (explicit):** Rigorous > Sound > Hand-wavy > Absent.
145	
146	**Gate:** Any criterion scored **Absent** fails the entire analysis — it must be revised and
147	re-scored, bounded to at most one re-perception pass per analysis, per "How to Apply This
148	Gate" above. If the criterion still scores Absent after that single pass, it is presented as
149	an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld, regardless of how
150	all other criteria score.
151	
152	**Hand-wavy cap:** Two or more criteria scored **Hand-wavy** also fails the entire analysis —
153	the same bound applies: revise and re-score once, per "How to Apply This Gate" above. One
154	criterion at Hand-wavy is tolerated (one isolated weaker section does not indicate a systemic
155	quality problem); two or more at Hand-wavy indicates a pattern of shallow reasoning that the
156	gate alone cannot catch, because no single criterion has reached the gate-fail level. If two or
157	more criteria still score Hand-wavy after that single pass, the cap breach is presented as an
158	unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld.
159	
160	**Pass:** No criterion scores Absent, and at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
161	(Equivalently: every criterion is Sound or above, except at most one may be Hand-wavy.)
162	
163	**Escape-valve scoring (global rule, applies to every criterion):** Any section that
164	legitimately uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`) is
165	scored **Rigorous** if the stated reason is specific to this analysis — it names a property
166	of this problem that makes the section's content unnecessary — and **Hand-wavy** if the
167	reason is generic or copy-pasteable to any analysis. A properly-used escape valve is
168	**never** scored Absent solely for using the escape valve: the per-criterion Absent
169	descriptors below apply to a section that is missing, empty, or filled with non-scoreable
170	content, not to a section that is honestly and specifically marked as having no material
171	content.
172	
173	**Load-bearing chain (definition):** A derivation chain is *load-bearing* if a claim in
174	the Conclusion section (output section 6) depends on it — i.e., the chain produces, or is
175	cited as support for, a conclusion the analysis actually presents. A chain that reaches
176	only an intermediate result no conclusion rests on is not load-bearing. (This is the
177	narrower scoring sense of the phrase `SKILL.md` uses informally as "load-bearing for a
178	high-stakes conclusion.")
