182	## Verdict Block Format
183	
184	The six verdict blocks are emitted together under the single top-level heading
185	`## Self-Audit Gate (process output)`, one `##` heading holding all six in criterion order —
186	the same placement the adversarial pass record and the self-audit scan prescribe for themselves.
187	They are one artifact, not six; nesting them beneath another section's heading makes them a
188	subsection of something they do not belong to, and a reader or a check keyed to that heading
189	must find it in the same structural position on every run.
190	
191	Each of the 6 criteria requires exactly one verdict block. Use the standard form when the
192	analysis section exists and contains scoreable content:
193	
194	```text
195	**Criterion N: [Criterion Name]**
196	Quoted span: "[Direct quote of the specific text that most directly determines the band assigned — from the analysis being scored, or, per the admission below, from the self-audit scan for Criteria 4 and 6 or the Assumption Audit scan for Criterion 2, each emitted as process output for this analysis.]"
197	Band: [**Rigorous** / **Sound** / **Hand-wavy** / **Absent**]
198	Justification: [One sentence tying the quoted span to the observable descriptor for
199	that band — name the specific structural property present or absent.]
200	```
201	
202	The self-audit scan and the Assumption Audit scan are not output sections, and they are the only artifacts outside the six-section analysis a verdict block may quote: the self-audit scan for Criteria 4 and 6, and the Assumption Audit scan for Criterion 2. Every other criterion quotes the analysis text itself, and the §6→§4 closure ledger is admitted nowhere — it is a drafting artifact that describes a document other than the one being scored.
203	
204	Use the gap-citation form when the criterion scores Absent because the section or named
205	artifact is missing or empty — in that case there is no span to quote, and the documented
206	absence is the evidence:
207	
208	```text
209	**Criterion N: [Criterion Name]**
210	Gap: [Name what is missing and where it should have appeared — e.g., "No Derivation
211	Chains section exists; chains of the form 'GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate] → [conclusion]'
212	should appear in section 4 (Derivation Chains) for each conclusion stated in section 6
213	(Conclusion)."]
214	Band: Absent
215	Justification: [One sentence: the absence itself is the structural failure that triggers
216	the gate — the criterion cannot be scored against a non-existent artifact.]
217	```
218	
219	Verdict blocks (not a consolidated table) are required because each block contains a quoted
220	span or a gap citation. Without that span, the evidence-quoting requirement cannot be audited:
221	a summary table of band labels can be produced by asserting compliance, but a verdict block
222	containing a quote that contradicts its claimed band creates a contradiction that cannot be
223	sustained.

227	## Criteria
228	
229	Apply all six criteria in the order listed. Criteria 1-5 follow the order of the
230	six-section output format — the same chain-of-artifacts sequence the analysis itself
231	follows — so that a scoring pass moves through the analysis in the order it was produced;
232	Criterion 6 is a whole-document cross-section check applied last.
233	
234	### Criterion 1: Identify Essence
235	
236	Scores the **Essence Statement** — the single sentence naming the core problem followed by
237	a short list of success criteria — in the Problem Essence section (output section 1).
238	
239	- **Rigorous** — the Essence Statement is a single sentence that names the core question or
240	  decision (not a symptom, not the triggering event, not a restatement of the user's prompt);
241	  each success criterion contains a pass/fail structural test — a verb + subject + outcome
242	  triplet where the outcome is a property of the Conclusion section — so that a reviewer
243	  applies each criterion by scanning the Conclusion section without analyst interpretation;
244	  the statement is specific enough that it appears nowhere in an analysis of a different but
245	  related problem without modification (it names a property unique to this problem, not a
246	  generic template phrase).
247	  If this section uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`), the
248	  stated reason is specific to this analysis's problem — it names a property of the problem
249	  that makes an Essence Statement unnecessary or redundant, and that reason appears in no
250	  other analysis without alteration.
251	
252	- **Sound** — the Essence Statement exists and names a question, but the success criteria are
253	  vague or stated in terms that cannot be verified against the conclusion without further
254	  clarification (e.g., "the solution should be good," "the approach should be appropriate").
255	
256	- **Hand-wavy** — the Essence Statement exists but names a symptom, a triggering event, or a
257	  restatement of the user's prompt rather than the underlying question; OR the success criteria
258	  are absent while the Essence Statement itself is present; OR the section uses the honest-depth
259	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
260	  "no essence was needed").
261	
262	- **Absent** — no Essence Statement is present (the Problem Essence section is empty, contains
263	  only a restatement of the original prompt with no analytical distillation, or the section
264	  heading appears with nothing below it).
265	  This verdict routes back to Phase 1 to re-frame the Essence Statement — or, when the cause is an input that was never supplied, to re-opening input under the Input Contract — rather than an in-place rewrite of output section 1; the route is bounded by the same rule described under `SKILL.md`'s "Before presenting conclusions" section.
266	
267	### Criterion 2: Challenge Assumptions
268	
269	Scores the **Classified Assumptions Table** — a table with columns Assumption, Type, Treatment,
270	Verdict, Verification — in the Assumptions Table section (output section 2). Folds in:
271	four-type classification quality and unverified-flag discipline (D-07).
272	
273	- **Rigorous** — every row in the Assumptions Table has a Type value drawn from exactly the
274	  four-type scheme (physical law / current constraint / convention / untested belief); the
275	  Treatment cell uses the vocabulary of the prescribed treatment for that type; the Verdict
276	  cell records Accept, Challenge, or Discard as a leading token followed by an em-dash and a
277	  specific justification — not the bare token alone; the Verification cell cites a specific
278	  source or names what verification confirms the assumption — not "unclear" or "possibly true";
279	  at least one assumption has been challenged (not merely labelled Accept); if any assumption
280	  is used in a derivation chain despite being unverified, the Verification cell reads
281	  "unverified — flagged"; the Assumption Audit performed at the end of Phase 4 (`SKILL.md`,
282	  "End-of-phase Assumption Audit") visited every named derivation chain step in section 4 and
283	  surfaced any assumption not already in the Assumptions Table, recording it there; the
284	  Assumption Audit artifact produced before scoring (per "How to Apply This Gate") confirms
285	  this scan was exhaustive over named derivation chain steps, not an open-ended survey of the
286	  universe of conceivable assumptions.
287	
288	- **Sound** — the table exists with populated rows, but one or more rows have generic entries:
289	  the Verification cell reads "unclear" or "unsure" without specifics, OR the Treatment
290	  cell records a treatment that does not match the prescribed treatment for the row's Type,
291	  OR one assumption that is used in a chain despite being unverified lacks the
292	  "unverified — flagged" notation.
293	
294	- **Hand-wavy** — the table exists but uses Type values outside the four-type scheme (e.g.,
295	  "general assumption," "business constraint," freeform labels); OR multiple rows have empty
296	  Verdict or Verification cells; OR every assumption is labelled Accept with no challenge
297	  attempted and no evidence cited for any verdict.
298	
299	- **Absent** — no Assumptions Table is present; OR the table exists but every row's Type
300	  cell is empty, freeform (no mapping to the four-type scheme), or missing — making the
301	  table a list of undifferentiated claims rather than a classified set.
302	
303	### Criterion 3: Establish Ground Truths
304	
305	Scores the **Ground Truths list** — a numbered list of verified facts with stable GT-IDs,
306	source citations, and a provenance label, with unverified and delegate-reported entries marked
307	with the `GT-N?` suffix — in the Ground Truths section (output section 3).
308	
309	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For
310	each unsuffixed ground truth, ask whether the analysis read the asserted figure in the cited
311	source — `read-at-source` — or merely received it from a sub-agent, search result, or summary
312	without opening the citation (`reported-by-delegate`, which requires the `?`). Score against
313	what the analysis did, not against how well-formed the citation looks.
314	
315	- **Rigorous** — every GT-item carries a stable identifier (GT-1, GT-2, etc.) that matches
316	  the identifiers referenced in the Derivation Chains section; every verified GT has a source
317	  citation that is more specific than "common knowledge" or "known fact"; every GT carries a
318	  provenance label; every unverified or delegate-reported GT is marked with the `?` suffix;
319	  the `?`-marked GTs are **enumerated by ID** and that enumeration matches the suffixed entries
320	  in the Ground Truths list when checked against it; every unsuffixed GT feeding a
321	  HIGH-confidence chain names its read-at-source location; no assumption that was discarded in
322	  Phase 2 (Verdict: Discard) appears in this list. Every unsuffixed GT whose cited source is
323	  reachable feeds at least one HIGH-confidence chain EXCEPT: the Phase 3 failure record names
324	  the source as unreachable, in which case the GT may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains, evidenced
325	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.
326	
327	  **Check the enumeration, do not quote it.** Quoting the analysis's own provenance summary as
328	  the satisfying span does not discharge this criterion — that verifies a summary was written,
329	  not that it is correct. Read the Ground Truths list, collect the IDs actually carrying `?`,
330	  and compare against the enumeration. Cite the comparison as the satisfying span (*"enumerated
331	  GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14; list carries `?` on exactly those four"*). Where a stated count and
332	  its enumeration disagree, the enumeration governs and the mismatched count is itself a defect.
333	
334	  **Reachability is decided by the Phase 3 record, not re-decided here.** A source is reachable
335	  when the Phase 3 verification step opened it, and unreachable when the Phase 3 failure record
336	  names it with a specific reason; the analyst reads the record and does not re-argue
337	  reachability per ground truth. This requirement is not satisfied by a ground truth that feeds
338	  no chain at all — a GT no derivation chain consumes is already a Criterion 4 defect, and the
339	  requirement presupposes at least one load-bearing chain consumes the GT. A single unsuffixed
340	  GT whose reachable source feeds only MEDIUM or LOW chains bands this criterion Sound; the same
341	  shortfall across multiple GTs bands it Hand-wavy.
342	
343	- **Sound** — GT-IDs are present and stable, but one or more verified GTs cite "common
344	  knowledge," "known fact," or no source at all; OR provenance labels are missing though the
345	  `?` suffixes themselves are correctly applied; OR one unread GT (unverified or
346	  delegate-reported) is used without the `?` suffix **and it feeds only MEDIUM or LOW
347	  confidence chains**; OR the `?`-marked GTs are summarized by a bare count rather than
348	  enumerated, though the suffixes in the list are themselves correct.
349	
350	  An enumeration that **disagrees with the list** does not band here — it bands **Hand-wavy**.
351	  A count that merely accompanies a correct enumeration and disagrees with it is a defect but
352	  bands Sound, since the enumeration governs and remains checkable.
353	
354	- **Hand-wavy** — GT-IDs are present but they are not stable (the same ID is used for
355	  different facts at different points in the document, or IDs are renumbered between sections);
356	  OR the list includes an assumption that was assigned a Discard verdict in Phase 2; OR
357	  multiple unread GTs are used in chains without the `?` suffix; OR **the `?` enumeration
358	  disagrees with the Ground Truths list** — an enumeration that omits a suffixed GT understates
359	  the analysis's unverified inputs in the direction that flatters it, and unlike a bare count it
360	  was checkable, so a mismatch is a stronger failure than never enumerating at all; OR **any
361	  unsuffixed GT feeds a HIGH-confidence chain without naming a read-at-source location** — a
362	  HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on a figure nobody read is the failure this criterion
363	  exists to catch, and a single instance is enough to land here.
364	
365	  **Fix — acquire before you downgrade.** Branch one, preferred: acquire the evidence — open
366	  the cited source, per the Phase 3 verification step, and let the read move the provenance
367	  label. Branch two: downgrade the confidence — carry the `?` and drop the chain from HIGH,
368	  taken only when the source cannot be opened or opens without containing the asserted figure or wording. The preference, explicitly: acquisition is preferred when the source is reachable, because a gate whose only available Fix weakens the output resolves every failure toward less claim rather than more evidence. The unreachable case is not a free pass — the downgrade branch still requires the Phase 3 failure record, which source and why unreachable, or `citation does not support the claim`, so a reader can tell a downgrade from a skipped attempt.
369	
370	- **Absent** — no GT-IDs are assigned to any fact in the Ground Truths section; OR the Ground
371	  Truths section lists claims without distinguishing verified from unverified (no `?` suffix
372	  appears anywhere, no citations appear anywhere, and the list is undifferentiated); OR the
373	  section is absent or empty.
374	
375	### Criterion 4: Reason Upward
376	
377	Scores **both** the **Derivation Chains** (output section 4) — one chain per conclusion,
378	formatted as `GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]` with at least one
379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
380	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
383	
384	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning
388	  section either documents
389	  at least one dead end using the What-was-tried / Why-abandoned / What-it-ruled-out structure,
390	  OR uses the honest-depth escape valve with a reason that is specific to this analysis's
391	  problem and appears in no other analysis without alteration; no analogy
392	  is used as direct evidence (any reference to how others solved a similar problem is grounded
393	  in a named GT about their situation, not offered as standalone justification);
394	  each chain step that introduces an assumption not already in the Assumptions Table
395	  declares that assumption inline using `[Assumes: X]` appended to the step text —
396	  a reviewer applies this check by scanning each chain step for the `[Assumes:` token;
397	  and every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by
398	  arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity
399	  cited to an unsuffixed ground truth — the test `output-template.md` states for the HIGH
400	  band under "Confidence levels, defined", shared here rather than restated. A hop that
401	  follows once the `[Assumes: X]` premise declared on that hop is granted counts as following
402	  for this criterion — declaring the premise takes the hop out of this limb by design, and
403	  whether that premise is priced is Criterion 5's Inference axis. An undeclared premise is not
404	  treated that way: a hop the endpoint depends on whose only gap is an undeclared premise is a
405	  non-sequitur under Hand-wavy below, and the `[Assumes: X]` limb above covers undeclared
406	  premises on hops the endpoint does not depend on; a hop citing
407	  a regularity to a `GT-N?` ground truth is an Inputs-axis matter Criterion 3/5 scores, not a
408	  failure to follow.
409	
410	- **Sound** — chains exist for all conclusions, but one or more chains lack a genuine
411	  intermediate step (the chain goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion, or the stated
412	  intermediate is a restatement of one of its named inputs rather than a new inference); OR
413	  a conclusion has more than one derivation chain — redundant restatement rather than a
414	  missing chain — where the prescribed form is exactly one chain per conclusion; OR
415	  one dead end in Abandoned Reasoning is described with a vague abandonment reason
416	  ("seemed unlikely," "ran out of time") rather than the specific structural reason
417	  (assumption false, contradicts a GT, circular, intermediate could not be established); OR
418	  one or more chains render their hops as an ordered list (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`) instead of the
419	  prescribed arrow-led hop form, OR break a single hop across physical lines rather than
420	  splitting it into two hops, which splits one chain into disconnected
421	  fragments even where every hop is individually sound; OR a hop fails to follow, or its
422	  arithmetic does not recompute, where the endpoint does not depend on that hop; OR a hop the
423	  endpoint depends on carries an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged — the
424	  only case of a hop the endpoint depends on that this band admits, and it covers arithmetic
425	  only: a hop the endpoint depends on that does not follow by deduction or cited regularity is
426	  Hand-wavy, whatever the grader judges its effect on the endpoint — **this clause is why the criterion
427	  cannot be scored on reasoning quality alone.** A chain that names its inputs, carries a
428	  genuine intermediate and reaches a conclusion satisfies every other Rigorous requirement
429	  while still failing the prescribed form; scoring only the semantics is what lets a
430	  Rigorous verdict coexist with a section of malformed chains.
431

464	  clause below, the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, or an explicit

480	  statement is the satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM, though its confidence
481	  line still gives each of its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account
482	  of why no available evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason; a

532	  or any clause other than the absent-fails one; OR a chain's head cites a chain marked

569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. 573	
574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. ## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Using the raw $70K headline as the decision number

**What was tried:** Early framing treated the $70K/yr figure itself as the quantity to weigh
against the partner's career cost.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1/GT-2/GT-4/GT-5/GT-8 once the Fermi estimate was run:
housing (C1) and commute (C3) costs alone remove $16K-$35K/yr from the figure before equity
is even discounted (C5). A raw headline comparison would have anchored the whole downstream
analysis on an inflated number.

**What it ruled out:** Treating the offer's top-line number as directly comparable to current
compensation without a cost-of-living pass — this is the single most common error in
relocation comp decisions and this dead end documents exactly why it fails here.

### Dead End: Assuming California taxes automatically cost more than Oregon's

**What was tried:** An initial pass (before the Oregon/Portland local-tax research) assumed
California's higher top marginal rate (13.3%) meant the move would increase the user's tax
burden, and priced that as a drag alongside housing.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1, GT-4, and GT-5: Oregon's 9.9% top bracket starts at
only $125,000, and Multnomah/Metro stack another 1-3% on top of that for Portland-area
residents, while California's comparable 9.3% bracket runs all the way to $371,479 with no
local personal-income-tax layer anywhere in the state (GT-6?). At the income band this
offer plausibly falls in, the "CA taxes more" framing reverses rather than merely weakens.

**What it ruled out:** Treating a state's headline top marginal rate as a proxy for an
individual taxpayer's actual burden without checking (a) the bracket thresholds at the
taxpayer's actual income and (b) local/county taxes layered on the "cheaper" state. This
also saves a future analyst from re-deriving the Oregon/Portland local-tax structure, which
is unusual and easy to miss.

**What was tried:** Framing the decision as primarily about whether 3 days/week in-office is
tolerable, implicitly treating the partner's situation as a secondary, office-cadence-driven
concern.

**Why abandoned:** The inversion/second-order pass (C7) and the partner-cost chain (C6) show
the forcing function is relocation itself, not the office-day count — a fully-remote offer
requiring the same relocation would create the identical partner-career problem. Anchoring on

**What it ruled out:** Negotiating only the in-office cadence (e.g., asking for 1-2 days
instead of 3) as if that alone resolves the household-level cost; it would not, unless paired
with a no-relocation or delayed-relocation arrangement.

the C4 economic bracket alone.

exactly the point Phase 2 exists to stop that.

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Decide from a bracketed real economic delta of roughly
$35K-$54K/yr before equity-discounting (chain C4) — not from the $70K headline and not from
the instinct that California taxes eat the raise (chain C2) — weighed against a currently
unpriced partner-career cost (chain C6) and against the fact that neither staying nor leaving
is actually risk-free (chain C7). Because the weight between cash upside and partner-career
cost is a personal value judgment this analysis cannot supply (chain C8), resolve it with
these concrete next steps rather than a verdict:

- Get the actual offer letter: confirm the cash/equity split, vesting schedule, and share
  type before trusting the $70K figure at all (chain C5).
- Get real rent quotes for 2-3 Bay Area neighborhoods within an acceptable commute of the new
  office, to replace C1's bracket with a real number (chain C1).
- Have your partner research, concretely, whether their field has any Bay Area opening,
  remote option, or licensing path — this single fact does more to resolve the decision than
  any further comp analysis (chain C6).
- Ask your current employer, directly, whether they would counter — it is a free option that
  changes the comparison on both sides (chain C7).
- As a couple, name your actual weight in your own words: would you rather have the cash/
  career upside or the relationship and location stability, and what would make you regret
  either choice in two years (chain C8, chain C9).

**Key insight:** The input most people assume is the big drag on a Portland-to-Bay-Area move
— California income tax — is, within the sourced data, roughly a wash or even a modest saving
at this income band, because Portland's local Metro and Multnomah County taxes stack on top
of Oregon's unusually low top-bracket threshold while California has no local personal income
tax anywhere in the state; the real drag is housing cost and commute time, not taxes

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: Incremental Bay Area housing cost is roughly $12K-$24K/yr, not zero

### Conclusion C2: The common "California taxes more" assumption is backwards at this income band

### Conclusion C7: Neither "stay remote" nor "relocate" is the risk-free option it is assumed to be

GT-9? (current role: fully remote, 5 years' tenure, user-stated)
→ inverting the implicit claim that staying is the safe default: a remote-work policy reversal (RTO mandate), a reorg that deprioritizes remote roles for promotion, or stagnant comp at the current employer would each make the status quo riskier than it looks today, and none of these has been ruled out [Assumes: A-16 — the current remote arrangement is not already protected by a signed, durable agreement]
→ second-order, actor lens: accepting the SF offer changes the current employer's incentives too — a competing offer is a live trigger for a counteroffer or retention adjustment, an option the user has not yet tested [Assumes: already tabled — the current employer would not counter-offer, see Assumptions Table]
→ second-order, time lens: immediately the move reads as a one-time cash/equity gain; after a few cycles the dominant effect shifts to whichever path builds more durable career capital (title, network, skill trajectory), a horizon this analysis cannot price without the user's own career goals [Assumes: A-17 — the user has a career-capital goal that matters independently of near-term comp]

### Conclusion C8: The decision resolves to a framework, not a single scored verdict

C4 (net economic delta, LOW) + C6 (partner-career cost, LOW) + C7 (reversibility/optionality, LOW) + GT-9? (offer terms) + GT-10? (partner's career)
→ a trade-off across the real option set — (a) stay remote in Portland, (b) relocate and have the partner quit/job-hunt in the Bay Area, (c) relocate and commute/live apart from the partner, (d) a composite option such as negotiating a reduced in-office cadence or a delayed-relocation trial period while the partner first explores Bay Area portability — is scoreable on economics (C4) but not yet on partner-cost (C6) or reversibility (C7), because those two criteria depend on facts only the user and partner hold

→ the decision therefore resolves to naming the priced known (C4's bracket), the named unknowns (C6, C7, GT-9?, GT-10?), and the specific questions that would let the couple supply the missing weights themselves — a framework rather than a single recommended option

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Using the raw $70K headline as the decision number

**What was tried:** Early framing treated the $70K/yr figure itself as the quantity to weigh
against the partner's career cost.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1/GT-2/GT-4/GT-5/GT-8 once the Fermi estimate was run:
housing (C1) and commute (C3) costs alone remove $16K-$35K/yr from the figure before equity
is even discounted (C5). A raw headline comparison would have anchored the whole downstream
analysis on an inflated number.

**What it ruled out:** Treating the offer's top-line number as directly comparable to current
compensation without a cost-of-living pass — this is the single most common error in
relocation comp decisions and this dead end documents exactly why it fails here.

### Dead End: Assuming California taxes automatically cost more than Oregon's

**What was tried:** An initial pass (before the Oregon/Portland local-tax research) assumed
California's higher top marginal rate (13.3%) meant the move would increase the user's tax
burden, and priced that as a drag alongside housing.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1, GT-4, and GT-5: Oregon's 9.9% top bracket starts at
only $125,000, and Multnomah/Metro stack another 1-3% on top of that for Portland-area
residents, while California's comparable 9.3% bracket runs all the way to $371,479 with no
local personal-income-tax layer anywhere in the state (GT-6?). At the income band this
offer plausibly falls in, the "CA taxes more" framing reverses rather than merely weakens.

**What it ruled out:** Treating a state's headline top marginal rate as a proxy for an
individual taxpayer's actual burden without checking (a) the bracket thresholds at the
taxpayer's actual income and (b) local/county taxes layered on the "cheaper" state. This
also saves a future analyst from re-deriving the Oregon/Portland local-tax structure, which
is unusual and easy to miss.

### Dead End: Treating the 3-days/week in-office requirement as the central obstacle

**What was tried:** Framing the decision as primarily about whether 3 days/week in-office is
tolerable, implicitly treating the partner's situation as a secondary, office-cadence-driven
concern.

**Why abandoned:** The inversion/second-order pass (C7) and the partner-cost chain (C6) show
the forcing function is relocation itself, not the office-day count — a fully-remote offer
requiring the same relocation would create the identical partner-career problem. Anchoring on
"3 days/week" understates the real decision variable.

**What it ruled out:** Negotiating only the in-office cadence (e.g., asking for 1-2 days
instead of 3) as if that alone resolves the household-level cost; it would not, unless paired
with a no-relocation or delayed-relocation arrangement.

### Dead End: Attempting to output a single prescriptive "accept" or "decline" verdict

**What was tried:** Drafting a direct recommendation ("take the offer" or "stay") based on
the C4 economic bracket alone.

**Why abandoned:** The trade-off procedure's weight-locking step (C8) could not be completed
honestly — the relative weight between cash upside and partner-career cost is a personal
value judgment resting on GT-9?/GT-10?, inputs this analysis was explicitly told to treat as
unknown rather than invent. Forcing a single verdict here would be reasoning by assumption at
exactly the point Phase 2 exists to stop that.

**What it ruled out:** A confident single-word recommendation that would look authoritative
but would actually be smuggling in an assumed answer to "how much do you value X over Y" that
only the user and partner can supply.

---

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Decide from a bracketed real economic delta of roughly
$35K-$58K/yr before equity-discounting (chain C4) — not from the $70K headline and not from
the instinct that California taxes eat the raise (chain C2) — weighed against a currently
unpriced partner-career cost (chain C6) and against the fact that neither staying nor leaving
is actually risk-free (chain C7). Because the weight between cash upside and partner-career
cost is a personal value judgment this analysis cannot supply (chain C8), resolve it with
these concrete next steps rather than a verdict:

- Get the actual offer letter: confirm the cash/equity split, vesting schedule, and share
  type before trusting the $70K figure at all (chain C5).
- Get real rent quotes for 2-3 Bay Area neighborhoods within an acceptable commute of the new
  office, to replace C1's bracket with a real number (chain C1).
- Have your partner research, concretely, whether their field has any Bay Area opening,
  remote option, or licensing path — this single fact does more to resolve the decision than
  any further comp analysis (chain C6).
- Ask your current employer, directly, whether they would counter — it is a free option that
  changes the comparison on both sides (chain C7).
- As a couple, name your actual weight in your own words: would you rather have the cash/
  career upside or the relationship and location stability, and what would make you regret
  either choice in two years (chain C8, chain C9).

**Key insight:** The input most people assume is the big drag on a Portland-to-Bay-Area move
— California income tax — is, within the sourced data, roughly a wash or even a modest saving
at this income band, because Portland's local Metro and Multnomah County taxes stack on top
of Oregon's unusually low top-bracket threshold while California has no local personal income
tax anywhere in the state; the real drag is housing cost and commute time, not taxes
(chain C2).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This analysis deliberately does not hand you a single "take it /
don't take it" answer — chain C8's weight-locking step cannot be completed without your and
your partner's own values and your partner's actual Bay Area job-market facts (chain C8).
Equity may also be worth meaningfully less than its quoted face value, so lead with the
cash-only portion of the delta until vesting terms are confirmed (chain C5).

exact comp split, equity terms, and in-office/location details — verification: obtain the
actual offer letter and vesting schedule) and GT-10? (the partner's real job-market

above, which only the user and partner can have). This LOW rating is not a defect to be

(rounded to "$4K-$11K" in the chain's own conclusion line — a rounding, not an error). C4: an
independent recompute of the combined bracket — using each component's own worst-case and
best-case ends together, not just their central values — gives 70-24-10.8-0=$35.2K at the
worst-case end and 70-12-3.6+3.8=$58.2K at the best-case end, matching the stated
$35K-$58K/yr bracket (central: 70-18-7.2+1.9=$46.7K, matching the stated ~$47K/yr). All
computed figures in this analysis recompute to their stated values; no arithmetic error
survived to this version.

**Sensitivity.** The single ground truth whose falsity would flip the headline finding (that
the tax drag is a wash/saving rather than a cost) is GT-6? — if California in fact permits,
or comes to permit, a local personal income tax (San Francisco's Board of Supervisors has
sought exactly this), chain C2's conclusion reverses and the tax column in C4 would become a
cost again rather than a credit. GT-6? is `?`-marked precisely because this was not verified
beyond convergent secondary sources. The weakest link across all nine chains is A-15 (the
assumed $150K-$370K income band in C2): the actual conclusion is income-level-dependent and
the user's real total comp was not supplied.

**Rival.** Headline conclusion (the realistic delta is $35K-$58K/yr, decided via a framework
rather than a verdict): the strongest rival is "the $70K headline is close enough to the real
number to just decide on" — ruled out by C1/C2/C3/C4's sourced arithmetic showing a
materially different bracket (see Abandoned Reasoning, "Using the raw $70K headline...").
C2 (tax finding): the strongest rival is "California taxes more, as commonly assumed" — ruled
out by GT-1/GT-2/GT-4/GT-5 directly (see Abandoned Reasoning, "Assuming California taxes
automatically cost more..."). C6 (partner cost): no live rival — no plausible reading of
GT-10? makes the partner's career cost zero; rival not applicable — the chain's claim
("this cost is real and unpriced") has no competing interpretation of the same ground truth.
C8 (framework-not-verdict): the strongest rival is "a weighted recommendation could have been
produced anyway, using reasonable default weights" — ruled out explicitly in Abandoned
Reasoning ("Attempting to output a single prescriptive verdict"), on the grounds that the
needed weights are a personal value judgment, not a fact this analysis holds.

**Premise.** The plan named in section 6 (get the offer letter, get rent quotes, have the
partner research portability, ask the current employer, name the couple's own weight) has
already failed to prevent a bad outcome two years on.

**Causes (unfiltered, from three stakeholder viewpoints).** From the user's viewpoint: the
equity underdelivered against the quoted face value (C5); the user never actually asked the
current employer for a counteroffer and will never know if one was available (C7); the user
over-weighted short-term cash and under-weighted career-capital trajectory, or the reverse
(C7). From the partner's viewpoint: the partner took a lower-leverage job in the Bay Area out
of time pressure rather than finding a genuine fit (C6); the partner never got a real say in
the weighting and went along with the move resentfully (C8); the commute/relocation ate into
family time neither partner priced in advance (C3). From a "competing employer" viewpoint
(adversarial): the new SF employer's hybrid policy tightens from 3 to 4-5 days within the
first year, after the household has already relocated and the leverage to renegotiate is gone;
the new employer's equity grant vests on a schedule back-loaded past the point the user would
realistically stay. From a "status-quo" viewpoint: the current employer, having lost the
negotiating leverage of a competing offer once the user leaves, would have offered a
retention package the user never tested; the current employer's own remote policy would have
held for the relevant horizon, making "staying" look safe in hindsight even though it wasn't
provably safe in advance.

**Clusters.** (1) Equity/comp underdelivery (bears on C5, GT-9?). (2) Partner-career cost
materializes larger than assumed (bears on C6, GT-10?). (3) Untested counterfactuals never
checked before committing — current-employer counteroffer, new-employer cadence creep (bears
on C7, A-16, A-17). (4) Decision made without the couple's own explicit weighting (bears on
C8).

**Disposition.** (1) Equity/comp underdelivery — mitigate: request the vesting schedule and
valuation basis before accepting (already named in chain C5 and in section 6's next steps);
accepted residual risk: equity markets and company performance cannot be fully hedged, named
explicitly as a caveat in section 6. (2) Partner-career cost — plan change: do not treat the
offer as decidable before the partner's Bay Area portability research (section 6's third
bullet) is actually done, not merely planned. (3) Untested counterfactuals — plan change: ask
the current employer directly before responding to the SF offer (section 6's fourth bullet),
converting an untested belief into a checked fact at near-zero cost. (4) No explicit
weighting — plan change: the couple's own weighting conversation (section 6's fifth bullet)
is treated as a precondition for deciding, not an optional afterthought.

**Falsification.** The conclusion (that the real economic delta is $35K-$58K/yr and the
decision should be resolved via the named framework rather than a single verdict) is false if
the user's actual offer letter and realistic neighborhood costs put the net delta clearly
outside this bracket (e.g., a fully-vested public-company RSU grant and a sub-$12K/yr housing
delta pushing the real gain above $60K/yr), or if the partner's career turns out to be fully
portable at no cost (in which case C6 collapses and a single verdict in favor of accepting
becomes defensible on the economics alone).

- "not from the $70K headline and not from the instinct that California taxes eat the raise" → chain C2 ✓

- "Get the actual offer letter: confirm the cash/equity split, vesting schedule, and share type" → chain C5 ✓
- "Get real rent quotes for 2-3 Bay Area neighborhoods within an acceptable commute" → chain C1 ✓
- "Have your partner research, concretely, whether their field has any Bay Area opening" → chain C6 ✓
- "Ask your current employer, directly, whether they would counter" → chain C7 ✓
- "As a couple, name your actual weight in your own words" → chain C8, chain C9 ✓
- "the real drag is housing cost and commute time, not taxes" (Key insight) → chain C2 ✓
- "chain C8's weight-locking step cannot be completed without your and your partner's own values" (Trade-offs acknowledged) → chain C8 ✓
- "Equity may also be worth meaningfully less than its quoted face value" (Trade-offs acknowledged) → chain C5 ✓
- "every chain contributing to this conclusion (C4, C6, C7, C8, C9) is rated below HIGH" (Confidence) → chains C4, C6, C7, C8, C9 ✓

All §6 claims cite a chain inline; no claim was cut.

tool_use_result.prompt:
Help a user reason through a personal career/relocation decision from first principles. This is not a coding task — it's a life decision analysis. Decompose the problem into verified ground truths, surface and challenge the hidden assumptions, and reason upward to a recommendation (or a clear framework for deciding, if the inputs are too personal/unknown for a single answer).

Situation:
- User is a software engineer, 5 years at their current employer, based in Portland, OR, currently in a fully remote role.
- A large San Francisco tech company has offered them a new job: +$70K/year total comp (base + equity combined) over current compensation.
- The new job requires relocating to the SF Bay Area and working 3 days/week in-office (hybrid).
- User's partner has an established, Portland-based career with no remote option for that partner's work — meaning relocation would force the partner to either quit, find a new job in the Bay Area, or the couple would need to commute/live apart.
- No other details given (ages, kids, savings, visa status, housing situation, how replaceable the partner's job is, risk tolerance, how much the user likes their current job, career trajectory goals, etc.) — treat unknowns as unknowns rather than inventing specifics.

What to do:
1. Decompose into the real underlying decision variables (comp delta after cost-of-living adjustment, career/equity upside, relationship/partner career cost, quality-of-life/commute cost, reversibility of the decision, optionality value of staying vs. going).
2. Apply inversion, second-order thinking, and a pre-mortem: what would make this decision obviously wrong in 2 years? What's being assumed that shouldn't be (e.g., that $70K raw delta is the real economic delta once SF Bay Area cost of living, taxes, and commute time are netted out; that equity is worth face value; that remote-with-no-equity-upside is a stable baseline; that the partner's career is truly non-transferable; that 3 days/week in-office is the binding constraint rather than the relocation itself).
3. Estimate the real magnitude of the comp delta after Bay Area cost-of-living adjustment (rent/housing especially) — rough Fermi estimate is fine, cite it as an estimate.
4. Surface the asymmetry: this is a two-body/joint decision, not just a personal comp optimization — the partner's career cost is a real economic and relational cost even though it doesn't show up in the offer letter.
5. Give a trade-off framing (not a prescriptive "yes take it" or "no don't") — the goal is to equip the user with the structure to decide, since only they know their risk tolerance, relationship priorities, and how replaceable the partner's job is.

Output format: a tight, readable analysis (not a wall of headers) ending in a short, concrete recommendation of what questions the user and their partner should answer together before deciding, plus a one-line bottom-line steer if the first-principles math points clearly one direction. Keep it under ~500 words — this will be relayed directly to the user in a chat, not stored as a document.

1	# Portland-to-Bay-Area Relocation Decision
2	
3	*First-principles analysis · 15 October 2026*
4	
5	*Read with: [How to read this analysis](HOW-TO-READ.md) · [Working file](analysis-20261015T044911Z.md) · [All files](INDEX.md)*
6	
7	## Executive Summary
8	
9	**Recommendation:** Decide from a real delta of ~$35K-$58K/yr, not the $70K headline
10	(chain C4) — weighed against an unpriced partner-career cost (chain C6) and the fact that
11	neither staying nor leaving is risk-free (chain C7). The cash-vs-partner weighting is a
12	judgment this analysis cannot supply (chain C8); use the five next steps in the Conclusion
13	instead of a verdict.
14	
15	**Band (from §6):** LOW — chains C4, C6, C7, C8, C9 are below HIGH; the conclusion rests on
16	unverified inputs GT-9? (offer terms) and GT-10? (partner's job portability).
17	
18	**Would change it:** The offer letter (chain C5), real rent quotes (chain C1), the partner's
19	job-market research (chain C6), the employer's counter-offer (chain C7), and the couple's own
20	weighting (chain C8).
21	
22	## 1. Problem Essence
23	
24	**Core problem:** Given a $70K/yr headline raise that requires relocating from Portland to the
25	SF Bay Area (hybrid, 3 days/week in-office) and would force the user's partner — whose
26	Portland-based career has no remote option — to either quit, job-hunt in the Bay Area, or
27	accept a commuting/living-apart arrangement, what is the real economic and household-level
28	trade-off, and what does the user (together with their partner) need to determine before
29	deciding?
30	
31	**Success criteria:**
32	1. States the realistic, cost-of-living-and-tax-adjusted economic delta of the offer (not the
33	   raw $70K figure), bracketed as an estimate with named inputs.
34	2. Treats the partner's career cost as a priced decision variable alongside the user's
35	   comp, not as an unpriced externality.
36	3. Surfaces and tests the hidden assumptions named in the task (stability of the remote
37	   baseline, true size of the CA tax drag, non-transferability of the partner's career,
38	   whether in-office cadence or relocation itself is the binding constraint) rather than
39	   accepting them at face value.
40	4. Produces either a single defensible recommendation or — if the personal/relational inputs
41	   are genuinely unknown — a concrete decision framework plus the specific questions the user
42	   and partner must answer to complete it. Both outcomes satisfy this criterion; the analysis
43	   is not required to name exactly one of "accept" or "decline" if a composite or
44	   conditional path (e.g., negotiated terms, a trial period) scores better.
45	5. Names the conditions under which the decision would look obviously wrong in two years
46	   (pre-mortem), for both the accept and decline paths.
47	
48	---
49	
50	## 2. Assumptions Table
51	
52	![Assumption verdict matrix: assumption types against verdicts](report-20261015T044911Z-fig-verdicts.svg)
53	
54	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
55	|------------|------|-----------|---------|--------------|
56	| The $70K/yr headline figure is the real economic gain from taking the offer | convention | Challenge before use — a quoted comp delta is pre-tax, pre-COL, pre-commute by convention, not by economic necessity | Challenge — survives only as an upper bound; net figure is materially lower once housing/commute are netted (see C1, C3, C4) | GT-8, Fermi estimate in C1/C3/C4 |
57	| Equity in the offer is worth its quoted/face value | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Challenge — unvested/illiquid equity conventionally carries a 20-40% discount; exact vesting/liquidity unknown | unverified — flagged (GT-9?); flagged in C5 |
58	| The current fully-remote role is a stable, indefinite baseline with no risk of its own | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Discard as stated — remote arrangements are revocable (RTO mandates, reorgs); "safe to stay" is not established | unverified — flagged; challenged via inversion in C7 |
59	| The 3-days/week in-office cadence is the binding cost of the new job, more than relocation itself | convention | Challenge before use | Discard as stated — relocation is the forcing function for the partner's career regardless of in-office day count | challenged via C6/C7 |
60	| The partner's career is genuinely non-transferable to the Bay Area | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Challenge — plausible as stated by the user but not independently verifiable by this analysis; portability (licensure, network, remote options at a Bay Area employer) is unknown | unverified — flagged (GT-10?); central input named in C6 and the Conclusion's next steps |
61	| California income tax is higher than Oregon's for this income band | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Discard — reversed by sourced data: Oregon's 9.9% top bracket starts at $125K and Multnomah/Metro add local tax on top, while CA's 9.3% bracket runs to $371,479 with no local personal income tax anywhere in the state | GT-1, GT-2, GT-3, GT-4, GT-5 (read-at-source); GT-6? (reported-by-delegate) — see C2 |
62	| Comparable Bay Area 2BR housing costs materially more than Portland | current constraint | Record expiry conditions — this is a real, current market condition, not a law; it would lift only if Bay Area housing supply/demand shifted sharply or the user chose an unusually cheap commute-accessible suburb | Accept — supported by sourced rent ranges; treated as a current market constraint, not permanent | GT-8 (read-at-source, affordwhere.com) |
63	| Time spent commuting has a nonzero personal opportunity cost | physical law | Accept as ground-truth candidate — time allocated to a commute cannot simultaneously be used for anything else; this is a conservation-of-time identity, not negotiable | Accept — definitional | GT-11 (identity); dollar value of that time is a separate, unverified estimate (see next row) |
64	| A commuter's time is worth $25-$50/hr for the purpose of pricing commute cost | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified — this is an assumed input to the Fermi estimate, not a measured figure | Challenge — plausible range, not sourced for this specific user; widens C3's bracket | unverified — flagged; used only inside C3's bracket, not presented as measured |
65	| No middle/composite option exists between "stay fully remote in Portland" and "relocate to the Bay Area" | convention | Challenge before use — the trade-off procedure requires testing composite/negotiated options before scoring named options alone | Challenge — a negotiated reduced cadence, delayed relocation, or trial period are live composite options not foreclosed by anything in the stated facts | named explicitly in C8's option set |
66	| This decision reduces to a single correct answer this analysis can supply | convention | Challenge before use | Discard as a universal claim — the weight the user places on partner-career-cost vs. cash upside is a personal value judgment this analysis cannot assert on the user's behalf | challenged in C8; drives the Conclusion's framework-not-verdict shape |
67	| The current employer would not counter-offer if the user raised the SF offer | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Challenge — untested; a live, cheap-to-test option | unverified — flagged; surfaced in C7 |
68	| The couple's willingness to live apart or have one partner job-hunt cold in a new market is already settled | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Challenge — not stated by the user; this is exactly the kind of relational fact Phase 2 requires flagging rather than assuming | unverified — flagged (GT-10?); named as a required next step in the Conclusion |
69	| [A-14] The incremental round-trip commute-time delta between the remote baseline and the hybrid role is roughly 60-90 minutes per in-office day | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Challenge — plausible range, not confirmed against the actual office location | unverified — flagged; surfaced in Phase 4 (C3), used only inside C3's bracket |
70	| [A-15] The user's total post-raise income falls in the ~$150,000-$370,000 single-filer band used in the OR/CA tax comparison | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Challenge — plausible for a 5-year senior engineer receiving a $70K raise, but not confirmed; if actual income sits below $125K or above $1M the comparison in C2 should be rerun | unverified — flagged; surfaced in Phase 4 (C2); confirming this would tighten C2/C4 |
71	| [A-16] The current fully-remote arrangement is not already protected by a signed, durable agreement (e.g., a contractual remote-work guarantee) | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Challenge — plausible default for most at-will US employment, not confirmed | unverified — flagged; surfaced in Phase 4 (C7) |
72	| [A-17] The user has a career-capital goal (title, network, or skill trajectory) that matters independently of near-term comp | untested belief | Verify, or flag unverified | Challenge — plausible for most engineers 5 years into a career, but not stated by the user; the weight this carries is exactly the kind of personal value judgment C8 flags | unverified — flagged; surfaced in Phase 4 (C7) |
73	
74	---
75	
76	## 3. Ground Truths
77	
78	- **GT-1** Oregon 2025 single-filer state income tax brackets: 4.75% ($0-$4,400), 6.75%
79	  ($4,400-$11,100), 8.75% ($11,100-$125,000), 9.9% (above $125,000) — source:

133	  = Raw Comp Delta − (Incremental Housing Cost + Incremental Commute-Time Cost + Incremental
134	  Tax Burden) ± Equity Valuation Adjustment — source: accounting identity, not an external
135	  citation; passes the irreducibility test as a definition rather than an empirical claim.

137	**Provenance summary:**
138	```text
