140	Read-at-source: GT-1 — brackets.tax Oregon-vs-California 2025 page, full bracket table
141	Read-at-source: GT-2 — brackets.tax Oregon-vs-California 2025 page, full bracket table
142	Read-at-source: GT-3 — edd.ca.gov Rates_and_withholding page, 2025 SDI rate and no-cap text
143	Read-at-source: GT-4 — multco.us/node/85310, PFA thresholds and rates
144	Read-at-source: GT-5 — portland.gov/revenue/personal-tax, SHS rate and threshold
145	Read-at-source: GT-8 — affordwhere.com/compare/portland-vs-san-francisco, rent ranges and overall %
146	```
147	
148	GT-6? and GT-9?/GT-10? were not read further this session: GT-6 because the specific
149	sfbos.org resolution PDF was not fetched directly (convergent secondary sources made the
150	underlying structural fact — no CA locality taxes personal income — high-confidence
151	without that extra fetch); GT-9/GT-10 because they describe the user's own private
152	situation and no external source exists for this analysis to open — they remain `?`
153	permanently until the user/partner confirm specifics, which the Conclusion names as a
154	required next step.
155	
156	---
157	
158	## 4. Derivation Chains
159	
160	![Evidence trace: ground truths, chains and the conclusion](report-20261015T044911Z-fig-trace.svg)
161	
162	### Conclusion C1: Incremental Bay Area housing cost is roughly $12K-$24K/yr, not zero
163	
164	GT-8 (Portland vs SF 1BR/2BR rent ranges, affordwhere.com)
165	→ a 2BR rents for roughly $1,830-$3,210/mo in Portland (midpoint ~$2,520) versus roughly $3,100-$5,900/mo in San Francisco proper (midpoint ~$4,500)
166	→ treating SF-proper rents as the upper end and a cheaper commute-accessible Bay Area suburb as the lower end brackets the monthly housing delta at roughly $1,000-$2,000, central ~$1,500
167	→ annualized across 12 months, this is an incremental housing cost of roughly $12,000-$24,000/yr, central ~$18,000/yr, that the raw $70K offer figure does not account for
168	
169	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — GT-8 is read at source but is a single real-estate aggregator's estimate rather than an authoritative government index, and the actual neighborhood/commute trade-off the user would choose is unknown; verification path: get an actual rent quote for 2-3 candidate Bay Area neighborhoods within an acceptable commute of the new office.
170	
171	### Conclusion C2: The common "California taxes more" assumption is backwards at this income band
172	
173	GT-1 (OR brackets) + GT-2 (CA brackets) + GT-3 (CA SDI 1.2%, uncapped) + GT-4 (Multnomah PFA) + GT-5 (Metro SHS) + GT-6? (CA bars local personal income tax statewide)
174	→ Oregon's state schedule reaches its 9.9% top bracket at just $125,000 of taxable income, a much lower threshold than California's 9.3% bracket, which runs from $72,724 to $371,479
175	→ Multnomah County and Metro each layer additional personal income tax (1.5%/3% and 1%) on income above that same $125,000 threshold, stacking directly onto the Oregon state rate for Portland-area residents
176	→ at representative upper-middle incomes the combined Oregon-plus-Portland-local marginal rate (about 12.4%-13.9%) exceeds California's combined state-plus-SDI marginal rate (about 10.5%) [Assumes: A-15 — total income falls in the ~$150K-$370K band, unconfirmed against GT-9?], because California has no local personal income tax anywhere in the state
177	→ a worked example at $270,000 total income shows Oregon+Portland owing about $28,600 in combined state+local tax versus California+SDI owing about $24,800 — roughly a $3,800/yr tax saving from relocating, the opposite of the common assumption that moving to California raises the tax bill
178	
179	**Confidence:** LOW — two axes are short at once, not one: GT-6? is `?`-marked (Inputs axis) — corroborated by convergent secondary sources but not read at its primary source; verification path: fetch the 2025 SF Board of Supervisors resolution directly or a California Franchise Tax Board confirmation that no locality may levy personal income tax. And the worked example's income band rests on A-15, a premise whose failure would shift this chain's conclusion rather than leave it intact (Inference axis) — verification path: confirm the user's actual total post-raise income. Two short axes at once caps this chain at LOW, not MEDIUM, per the confidence-band definition.
180	
181	### Conclusion C3: Hybrid in-office commuting adds a real but soft annual cost of roughly $4K-$11K/yr
182	
183	GT-9? (offer terms: 3 days/week hybrid, user-stated)
184	→ assuming a round-trip commute delta of roughly 60-90 minutes/day versus the current zero-commute remote baseline, 3 days/week across about 48 working weeks/year totals roughly 144-216 hours/year of new commute time [Assumes: A-14 — commute-time delta of 60-90 min/day round trip, not confirmed against a specific office location]
185	→ valuing that time at $25-$50/hr, a personal-time opportunity-cost range rather than a measured wage rate, yields an incremental annual commute cost of roughly $3,600-$10,800/yr, central ~$7,000/yr
186	→ hybrid in-office work therefore adds a real, if soft, annual cost of roughly $4K-$11K/yr that a cash-comp comparison omits entirely
187	
188	**Confidence:** LOW — rests directly on GT-9? (the offer's exact in-office cadence and location are user-stated, unconfirmed against an offer letter) and on two further unverified estimate inputs (commute-time delta, value-of-time range) with no cited source for either; verification path: confirm the actual office location/commute distance and, separately, decide what hourly value the user and partner actually place on personal time.
189	
190	### Conclusion C4: The realistic net economic delta, before equity-discounting, is roughly $35K-$58K/yr — not $70K
191	
192	C1 (housing delta, MEDIUM) + C2 (tax finding, LOW) + C3 (commute cost, LOW) + GT-9? (offer: +$70K raw) + GT-11 (net-delta identity)
193	→ applying GT-11's identity and combining C1's housing drag ($12K-$24K/yr), C3's commute drag ($3.6K-$10.8K/yr), and C2's tax effect (a $0-$3.8K/yr saving, credited rather than debited) against the $70K raw figure at their respective worst-case and best-case ends nets to a real economic delta bracket of roughly $35K-$58K/yr, central ~$47K/yr
194	→ this is substantially below the $70K headline, but also higher than the "taxes alone cut it by a third" intuition would predict, because the single largest assumed drag — California income tax — is not actually a drag at this income band
195	
196	**Confidence:** LOW — capped by C2 and C3 (both LOW) on its head and by GT-9? directly; C1's verification path (actual neighborhood rent quotes), C2's (confirm GT-6? and the user's real income level, A-15), and C3's (confirm commute distance and time-value) together would tighten this bracket; until then, treat $35K-$58K/yr as a bracket, not a point estimate.
197	
198	### Conclusion C5: The equity component may be worth materially less than its quoted face value
199	
200	GT-9? (offer includes equity as part of the +$70K, user-stated)
201	→ equity in a compensation offer is conventionally quoted at a face/grant value that assumes full vesting and no share-price decline, both of which are uncertain for an offer whose company, share type (public RSU vs. private/illiquid), and vesting schedule were not supplied
202	→ applying a conventional 20-40% illiquidity/vesting/volatility discount to just the equity share of the figure, an unknown fraction of the $70K, further reduces the realistic annual value of the raise by an amount this analysis cannot size without that split
203	→ C4's $35K-$58K/yr bracket should be read as an upper estimate until the equity's vesting schedule and share type are confirmed; the cash-only portion of the delta is the more reliable number to act on in the meantime
204	
205	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — the discount convention itself is well-established in comp analysis (Inference axis is sound); the only shortfall is GT-9? (the cash/equity split and vesting terms are unconfirmed); verification path: request the equity grant's vesting schedule, share type, and current valuation basis from the offer letter.
206	
207	### Conclusion C6: The partner's career cost is a real, currently-unpriced household cost
208	
209	GT-10? (partner's established, non-remote Portland career, user-stated)
210	→ an offer's compensation figure prices only the offer-holder's individual labor-market value; it carries no accounting for a second household member's income, seniority, or professional network
211	→ when relocation forces a partner to quit, restart in a new market, or sustain a long-distance arrangement, the household absorbs a cost — lost income during a job search, lost seniority/network value, or the relational strain of living apart — that does not appear anywhere in C4's bracket
212	→ C4's $35K-$58K/yr figure is therefore a one-person economic view; the true household-level expected value nets out a partner-career cost whose size depends on facts this analysis was explicitly not given
213	
214	**Confidence:** LOW — rests directly on GT-10?, which names an input (the partner's actual job-market portability) with no verification path available to this analysis at all; only the user and partner can supply it, which is why the Conclusion routes this to a named next step rather than to a number.
215	
216	### Conclusion C7: Neither "stay remote" nor "relocate" is the risk-free option it is assumed to be
217	
218	GT-9? (current role: fully remote, 5 years' tenure, user-stated)
219	→ inverting the implicit claim that staying is the safe default: a remote-work policy reversal (RTO mandate), a reorg that deprioritizes remote roles for promotion, or stagnant comp at the current employer would each make the status quo riskier than it looks today, and none of these has been ruled out [Assumes: A-16 — the current remote arrangement is not already protected by a signed, durable agreement]
220	→ second-order, actor lens: accepting the SF offer changes the current employer's incentives too — a competing offer is a live trigger for a counteroffer or retention adjustment, an option the user has not yet tested [Assumes: already tabled — the current employer would not counter-offer, see Assumptions Table]
221	→ second-order, time lens: immediately the move reads as a one-time cash/equity gain; after a few cycles the dominant effect shifts to whichever path builds more durable career capital (title, network, skill trajectory), a horizon this analysis cannot price without the user's own career goals [Assumes: A-17 — the user has a career-capital goal that matters independently of near-term comp]
222	→ "staying" is not a risk-free baseline and "leaving" is not simply a risk weighed against a safe default; both paths carry real, differently-shaped risk that the headline comp numbers do not capture
223	
224	**Confidence:** LOW — rests on GT-9? and on three untested beliefs (A-16, A-17, and the already-tabled employer-counteroffer belief) about remote-work durability, career-capital goals, and counteroffer likelihood, neither with a verification path available except asking the current employer directly and the user naming their own career goals, which the Conclusion names as a next step.
225	
226	### Conclusion C8: The decision resolves to a framework, not a single scored verdict
227	
228	C4 (net economic delta, LOW) + C6 (partner-career cost, LOW) + C7 (reversibility/optionality, LOW) + GT-9? (offer terms) + GT-10? (partner's career)
229	→ a trade-off across the real option set — (a) stay remote in Portland, (b) relocate and have the partner quit/job-hunt in the Bay Area, (c) relocate and commute/live apart from the partner, (d) a composite option such as negotiating a reduced in-office cadence or a delayed-relocation trial period while the partner first explores Bay Area portability — is scoreable on economics (C4) but not yet on partner-cost (C6) or reversibility (C7), because those two criteria depend on facts only the user and partner hold
230	→ locking criterion weights before scoring, the trade-off procedure's core discipline, is not honestly possible here: the weight the user would place on partner career cost versus cash upside is itself the personal value judgment the decision turns on, not a fact this analysis can assert on the user's behalf
231	→ the decision therefore resolves to naming the priced known (C4's bracket), the named unknowns (C6, C7, GT-9?, GT-10?), and the specific questions that would let the couple supply the missing weights themselves — a framework rather than a single recommended option
232	
233	**Confidence:** LOW — every input this chain cites is itself LOW or `?`-marked; this is not a weakness to be fixed by more analysis, it is the honest shape of a decision whose two highest-weighted criteria are facts only the user and partner can supply (see Conclusion for the specific questions).
234	
235	### Conclusion C9: Pre-mortem — both paths have a specific, plausible failure story
236	
237	C4 (net economic delta, LOW) + C6 (partner-career cost, LOW) + C7 (reversibility/optionality, LOW)
238	→ running a pre-mortem on "we accepted the offer and it was a mistake" surfaces a recurring cluster: the equity/comp upside underdelivers (C5), the partner's career cost turns out larger than assumed because the Bay Area market doesn't want their skillset or they take a lower-leverage job (C6), and the relationship absorbs a living-apart or resentment cost the move's cash gain doesn't offset
239	→ running the mirror pre-mortem on "we stayed and it was a mistake" surfaces: remote work gets rescinded anyway at the current employer, promotion/comp stagnate, and the user regrets never testing the counteroffer or market rate the SF offer revealed (C7)
240	→ both paths have a plausible, specific failure story, which is itself evidence this is a genuine trade-off rather than a decision with a dominant answer; the pre-mortem's practical value is in naming the tripwires worth checking before committing either way — did the current employer counter, is there an actual Bay-Area opening in the partner's field, does the equity vest on the schedule quoted
241	
242	**Confidence:** LOW — built entirely from LOW-rated chains; its value is diagnostic (naming tripwires) rather than predictive, and it is not cited by any other chain's head.
243	
244	---
245	
246	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
247	
248	### Dead End: Using the raw $70K headline as the decision number
249	
250	**What was tried:** Early framing treated the $70K/yr figure itself as the quantity to weigh
251	against the partner's career cost.
252	
253	**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1/GT-2/GT-4/GT-5/GT-8 once the Fermi estimate was run:
254	housing (C1) and commute (C3) costs alone remove $16K-$35K/yr from the figure before equity
255	is even discounted (C5). A raw headline comparison would have anchored the whole downstream
256	analysis on an inflated number.
257	
258	**What it ruled out:** Treating the offer's top-line number as directly comparable to current
259	compensation without a cost-of-living pass — this is the single most common error in
260	relocation comp decisions and this dead end documents exactly why it fails here.
261	
262	### Dead End: Assuming California taxes automatically cost more than Oregon's
263	
264	**What was tried:** An initial pass (before the Oregon/Portland local-tax research) assumed
265	California's higher top marginal rate (13.3%) meant the move would increase the user's tax
266	burden, and priced that as a drag alongside housing.
267	
268	**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1, GT-4, and GT-5: Oregon's 9.9% top bracket starts at
269	only $125,000, and Multnomah/Metro stack another 1-3% on top of that for Portland-area
270	residents, while California's comparable 9.3% bracket runs all the way to $371,479 with no
271	local personal-income-tax layer anywhere in the state (GT-6?). At the income band this
272	offer plausibly falls in, the "CA taxes more" framing reverses rather than merely weakens.
273	
274	**What it ruled out:** Treating a state's headline top marginal rate as a proxy for an
275	individual taxpayer's actual burden without checking (a) the bracket thresholds at the
276	taxpayer's actual income and (b) local/county taxes layered on the "cheaper" state. This
277	also saves a future analyst from re-deriving the Oregon/Portland local-tax structure, which
278	is unusual and easy to miss.
279	
280	### Dead End: Treating the 3-days/week in-office requirement as the central obstacle
281	
282	**What was tried:** Framing the decision as primarily about whether 3 days/week in-office is
283	tolerable, implicitly treating the partner's situation as a secondary, office-cadence-driven
284	concern.
285	
286	**Why abandoned:** The inversion/second-order pass (C7) and the partner-cost chain (C6) show
287	the forcing function is relocation itself, not the office-day count — a fully-remote offer
288	requiring the same relocation would create the identical partner-career problem. Anchoring on
289	"3 days/week" understates the real decision variable.
290	
291	**What it ruled out:** Negotiating only the in-office cadence (e.g., asking for 1-2 days
292	instead of 3) as if that alone resolves the household-level cost; it would not, unless paired
293	with a no-relocation or delayed-relocation arrangement.
294	
295	### Dead End: Attempting to output a single prescriptive "accept" or "decline" verdict
296	
297	**What was tried:** Drafting a direct recommendation ("take the offer" or "stay") based on
298	the C4 economic bracket alone.
299	
300	**Why abandoned:** The trade-off procedure's weight-locking step (C8) could not be completed
301	honestly — the relative weight between cash upside and partner-career cost is a personal
302	value judgment resting on GT-9?/GT-10?, inputs this analysis was explicitly told to treat as
303	unknown rather than invent. Forcing a single verdict here would be reasoning by assumption at
304	exactly the point Phase 2 exists to stop that.
305	
306	**What it ruled out:** A confident single-word recommendation that would look authoritative
307	but would actually be smuggling in an assumed answer to "how much do you value X over Y" that
308	only the user and partner can supply.
309	
310	---
311	
312	## 6. Conclusion
313	
314	**Recommended approach:** Decide from a bracketed real economic delta of roughly
315	$35K-$58K/yr before equity-discounting (chain C4) — not from the $70K headline and not from
316	the instinct that California taxes eat the raise (chain C2) — weighed against a currently
317	unpriced partner-career cost (chain C6) and against the fact that neither staying nor leaving
318	is actually risk-free (chain C7). Because the weight between cash upside and partner-career
319	cost is a personal value judgment this analysis cannot supply (chain C8), resolve it with
320	these concrete next steps rather than a verdict:
321	
322	- Get the actual offer letter: confirm the cash/equity split, vesting schedule, and share
323	  type before trusting the $70K figure at all (chain C5).
324	- Get real rent quotes for 2-3 Bay Area neighborhoods within an acceptable commute of the new
325	  office, to replace C1's bracket with a real number (chain C1).
326	- Have your partner research, concretely, whether their field has any Bay Area opening,
327	  remote option, or licensing path — this single fact does more to resolve the decision than
328	  any further comp analysis (chain C6).
329	- Ask your current employer, directly, whether they would counter — it is a free option that
330	  changes the comparison on both sides (chain C7).
331	- As a couple, name your actual weight in your own words: would you rather have the cash/
332	  career upside or the relationship and location stability, and what would make you regret
333	  either choice in two years (chain C8, chain C9).
334	
335	**Key insight:** The input most people assume is the big drag on a Portland-to-Bay-Area move
336	— California income tax — is, within the sourced data, roughly a wash or even a modest saving
337	at this income band, because Portland's local Metro and Multnomah County taxes stack on top
338	of Oregon's unusually low top-bracket threshold while California has no local personal income
339	tax anywhere in the state; the real drag is housing cost and commute time, not taxes
340	(chain C2).
341	
342	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This analysis deliberately does not hand you a single "take it /
343	don't take it" answer — chain C8's weight-locking step cannot be completed without your and
344	your partner's own values and your partner's actual Bay Area job-market facts (chain C8).
345	Equity may also be worth meaningfully less than its quoted face value, so lead with the
346	cash-only portion of the delta until vesting terms are confirmed (chain C5).
347	
348	**Confidence:** LOW — every chain contributing to this conclusion (C4, C6, C7, C8, C9) is
349	rated below HIGH, each with its own verification path stated on its own confidence line in
350	section 4. The Conclusion also rests directly on two unverified inputs: GT-9? (the offer's
351	exact comp split, equity terms, and in-office/location details — verification: obtain the
352	actual offer letter and vesting schedule) and GT-10? (the partner's real job-market
353	portability and the couple's willingness to live apart — verification: the conversation named
354	above, which only the user and partner can have). This LOW rating is not a defect to be
355	fixed by more analysis — chain C8 explains why the two highest-weighted inputs here are
356	facts only the user and partner can supply.

# Portland-to-Bay-Area Relocation Decision

*First-principles analysis · 15 October 2026*

*Read with: [How to read this analysis](HOW-TO-READ.md) · [Working file](analysis-20261015T044911Z.md) · [All files](INDEX.md)*

## Executive Summary

**Recommendation:** Decide from a real delta of ~$35K-$58K/yr, not the $70K headline
(chain C4) — weighed against an unpriced partner-career cost (chain C6) and the fact that
neither staying nor leaving is risk-free (chain C7). The cash-vs-partner weighting is a
judgment this analysis cannot supply (chain C8); use the five next steps in the Conclusion
instead of a verdict.

**Band (from §6):** LOW — chains C4, C6, C7, C8, C9 are below HIGH; the conclusion rests on
unverified inputs GT-9? (offer terms) and GT-10? (partner's job portability).

**Would change it:** The offer letter (chain C5), real rent quotes (chain C1), the partner's
job-market research (chain C6), the employer's counter-offer (chain C7), and the couple's own
weighting (chain C8).

## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Given a $70K/yr headline raise that requires relocating from Portland to the
SF Bay Area (hybrid, 3 days/week in-office) and would force the user's partner — whose
Portland-based career has no remote option — to either quit, job-hunt in the Bay Area, or
accept a commuting/living-apart arrangement, what is the real economic and household-level
trade-off, and what does the user (together with their partner) need to determine before
deciding?

**Success criteria:**
1. States the realistic, cost-of-living-and-tax-adjusted economic delta of the offer (not the
   raw $70K figure), bracketed as an estimate with named inputs.
2. Treats the partner's career cost as a priced decision variable alongside the user's
   comp, not as an unpriced externality.
3. Surfaces and tests the hidden assumptions named in the task (stability of the remote
   baseline, true size of the CA tax drag, non-transferability of the partner's career,
   whether in-office cadence or relocation itself is the binding constraint) rather than
   accepting them at face value.
4. Produces either a single defensible recommendation or — if the personal/relational inputs
   are genuinely unknown — a concrete decision framework plus the specific questions the user
   and partner must answer to complete it. Both outcomes satisfy this criterion; the analysis
   is not required to name exactly one of "accept" or "decline" if a composite or
   conditional path (e.g., negotiated terms, a trial period) scores better.
5. Names the conditions under which the decision would look obviously wrong in two years
   (pre-mortem), for both the accept and decline paths.

---

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Using the raw $70K headline as the decision number

**What was tried:** Early framing treated the $70K/yr figure itself as the quantity to weigh
against the partner's career cost.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1/GT-2/GT-4/GT-5/GT-8 once the Fermi estimate was run:
housing (C1) and commute (C3) costs alone remove $16K-$35K/yr from the figure before equity
is even discounted (C5). A raw headline comparison would have anchored the whole downstream
analysis on an inflated number.

**What it ruled out:** Treating the offer's top-line number as directly comparable to current
compensation without a cost-of-living pass — this is the single most common error in
relocation comp decisions and this dead end documents exactly why it fails here.

### Dead End: Assuming California taxes automatically cost more than Oregon's

**What was tried:** An initial pass (before the Oregon/Portland local-tax research) assumed
California's higher top marginal rate (13.3%) meant the move would increase the user's tax
burden, and priced that as a drag alongside housing.

**Why abandoned:** Contradicted by GT-1, GT-4, and GT-5: Oregon's 9.9% top bracket starts at
only $125,000, and Multnomah/Metro stack another 1-3% on top of that for Portland-area
residents, while California's comparable 9.3% bracket runs all the way to $371,479 with no
local personal-income-tax layer anywhere in the state (GT-6?). At the income band this
offer plausibly falls in, the "CA taxes more" framing reverses rather than merely weakens.

**What it ruled out:** Treating a state's headline top marginal rate as a proxy for an
individual taxpayer's actual burden without checking (a) the bracket thresholds at the
taxpayer's actual income and (b) local/county taxes layered on the "cheaper" state. This
also saves a future analyst from re-deriving the Oregon/Portland local-tax structure, which
is unusual and easy to miss.

### Dead End: Treating the 3-days/week in-office requirement as the central obstacle

**What was tried:** Framing the decision as primarily about whether 3 days/week in-office is
tolerable, implicitly treating the partner's situation as a secondary, office-cadence-driven
concern.

**Why abandoned:** The inversion/second-order pass (C7) and the partner-cost chain (C6) show
the forcing function is relocation itself, not the office-day count — a fully-remote offer
requiring the same relocation would create the identical partner-career problem. Anchoring on
"3 days/week" understates the real decision variable.

**What it ruled out:** Negotiating only the in-office cadence (e.g., asking for 1-2 days
instead of 3) as if that alone resolves the household-level cost; it would not, unless paired
with a no-relocation or delayed-relocation arrangement.

### Dead End: Attempting to output a single prescriptive "accept" or "decline" verdict

**What was tried:** Drafting a direct recommendation ("take the offer" or "stay") based on
the C4 economic bracket alone.

**Why abandoned:** The trade-off procedure's weight-locking step (C8) could not be completed
honestly — the relative weight between cash upside and partner-career cost is a personal
value judgment resting on GT-9?/GT-10?, inputs this analysis was explicitly told to treat as
unknown rather than invent. Forcing a single verdict here would be reasoning by assumption at
exactly the point Phase 2 exists to stop that.

**What it ruled out:** A confident single-word recommendation that would look authoritative
but would actually be smuggling in an assumed answer to "how much do you value X over Y" that
only the user and partner can supply.

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Decide from a bracketed real economic delta of roughly
$35K-$58K/yr before equity-discounting (chain C4) — not from the $70K headline and not from
the instinct that California taxes eat the raise (chain C2) — weighed against a currently
unpriced partner-career cost (chain C6) and against the fact that neither staying nor leaving
is actually risk-free (chain C7). Because the weight between cash upside and partner-career
cost is a personal value judgment this analysis cannot supply (chain C8), resolve it with
these concrete next steps rather than a verdict:

- Get the actual offer letter: confirm the cash/equity split, vesting schedule, and share
  type before trusting the $70K figure at all (chain C5).
- Get real rent quotes for 2-3 Bay Area neighborhoods within an acceptable commute of the new
  office, to replace C1's bracket with a real number (chain C1).
- Have your partner research, concretely, whether their field has any Bay Area opening,
  remote option, or licensing path — this single fact does more to resolve the decision than
  any further comp analysis (chain C6).
- Ask your current employer, directly, whether they would counter — it is a free option that
  changes the comparison on both sides (chain C7).
- As a couple, name your actual weight in your own words: would you rather have the cash/
  career upside or the relationship and location stability, and what would make you regret
  either choice in two years (chain C8, chain C9).

**Key insight:** The input most people assume is the big drag on a Portland-to-Bay-Area move
— California income tax — is, within the sourced data, roughly a wash or even a modest saving
at this income band, because Portland's local Metro and Multnomah County taxes stack on top
of Oregon's unusually low top-bracket threshold while California has no local personal income
tax anywhere in the state; the real drag is housing cost and commute time, not taxes
(chain C2).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This analysis deliberately does not hand you a single "take it /
don't take it" answer — chain C8's weight-locking step cannot be completed without your and
your partner's own values and your partner's actual Bay Area job-market facts (chain C8).
Equity may also be worth meaningfully less than its quoted face value, so lead with the
cash-only portion of the delta until vesting terms are confirmed (chain C5).

**Confidence:** LOW — every chain contributing to this conclusion (C4, C6, C7, C8, C9) is
rated below HIGH, each with its own verification path stated on its own confidence line in

Here's the first-principles breakdown (the subagent did the research — tax brackets, rent data, etc. — rather than me guessing):

**The $70K headline isn't the real number.** Once you net out the actual costs the raw figure ignores:

- **Housing:** Bay Area rent runs roughly $12K–24K/yr more than Portland for a comparable 2BR, even picking a cheaper commute-accessible suburb rather than SF proper.
- **Commute:** 3 days/week in-office at a plausible 60–90 min round trip adds ~$4K–11K/yr in opportunity cost (at $25–50/hr value of time).
- **Taxes — the surprise:** The common assumption that California taxes eat the raise is backwards at this income level. Oregon's 9.9% top bracket kicks in at just $125K, and Multnomah County + Metro stack another 1–3% local tax on top of that for Portland residents. California has no local income tax anywhere in the state. Net effect: moving is roughly tax-*neutral to slightly favorable*, not a drag.
- **Equity:** Whatever portion of the $70K is equity (unknown split) conventionally deserves a 20–40% haircut for vesting/illiquidity risk until you see the actual grant terms.

**Net result: the real economic upside is more like $35K–58K/yr, not $70K** — still positive, just a third smaller than it looks on paper.

**The bigger issue isn't the office days — it's the move itself.** A fully-remote version of this same offer would still force the identical choice for your partner. Treating "3 days/week" as the sticking point understates the actual decision, which is a two-career household problem, not a comp problem. That cost doesn't show up in any offer letter, and only you two can price it.

**Also worth inverting:** staying isn't risk-free either. "Fully remote, 5 years in" can end with one RTO memo or reorg — it's not a guaranteed stable baseline, and you haven't tested whether your current employer would counter.

**Bottom line:** this doesn't resolve to a clean yes/no — the two inputs that actually decide it (your partner's real portability in the Bay Area job market, and how much weight you two put on cash/career upside vs. relationship and location stability) aren't things I can supply. Before deciding, I'd get:

1. The actual offer letter — cash/equity split, vesting, share type.
2. Real rent quotes for 2–3 candidate neighborhoods near the office.
3. Your partner's honest read on whether their field has *any* Bay Area opening, remote option, or licensing path — this one fact moves the decision more than anything else here.
4. A test of whether your current employer would counter.
5. A direct conversation with your partner: cash/career upside vs. stability — and what would make each of you regret the other choice in two years.
